ib-tok-exhibition-help.programmesIntro: Theory of Knowledge exists only in the Diploma Programme, but the habits it tests are built earlier and the word "exhibition" appears in two different programmes. Parents regularly book TOK support for a child who is actually facing the PYP exhibition, which is a different task with different rules.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: TOK runs across both DP years as a core requirement alongside the Extended Essay and CAS. The exhibition is normally taught and submitted in DP1; the TOK essay, written against one of six prescribed titles released by the IB, belongs to DP2. The exhibition carries one third of the TOK grade and the essay the other two thirds, and the two together with the Extended Essay decide up to three points on top of the six subject grades.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools schedule the exhibition unusually early, often finishing it before the DP1 summer, because the second year is crowded with Internal Assessments and the Extended Essay. That compresses the whole task into one or two terms. A DP1 student in Dubai or Abu Dhabi who starts thinking about objects in the week the deadline is announced has already lost the planning weeks that make the commentary easy to write.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP has no TOK and no exhibition. Its capstone is the Personal Project in MYP Year 5, assessed against its own criteria, plus interdisciplinary units that ask students to connect subjects. The transferable skill is the one the exhibition later needs: making a claim about an object or a source and then justifying it with evidence rather than opinion. Students who were never pushed on that in MYP find the exhibition's justification requirement genuinely new.
programmes.countryNote: A large share of UAE IB schools run MYP straight into DP, so the gap between a Personal Project in May and TOK objects the following January can be eight months. Where a school instead offers IGCSE in Years 10 and 11, students arrive in DP1 having been assessed almost entirely on recall and method, and the exhibition is the first task that asks them to argue about knowledge itself.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP exhibition is the Year 6 culminating project: a collaborative inquiry presented to the school community, assessed against the programme's own expectations rather than any IB mark scheme. It shares a name with the TOK exhibition and nothing else. There is no 950-word ceiling, no IA prompt, no external moderation and no contribution to a diploma grade. Support looks like inquiry coaching and presentation practice, not commentary review.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai and Abu Dhabi schools run PYP exhibitions in the spring term, which is why a parent searching for exhibition support in February may be looking at either task. If your child is in Year 6, the page you want is about inquiry and presentation. If your child is in DP1 and a TOK teacher has mentioned IA prompts, you are in the right place.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The CP core includes Personal and Professional Skills, a Reflective Project, language development and service learning. It does not include Theory of Knowledge, so CP students never sit an exhibition or a TOK essay. The Reflective Project asks for an ethical dilemma arising from the student's career-related study, which has a surface resemblance to TOK and a completely different assessment structure.
programmes.countryNote: CP is offered by only a handful of UAE schools, which is why its requirements are frequently misdescribed in tutoring enquiries. If your child is on CP and has been asked for objects and an IA prompt, check with the DP coordinator before booking anything: either the school runs both programmes and the message was for a DP cohort, or the task has been misnamed.

ib-tok-exhibition-help.subjectsIntro: The exhibition is anchored in one TOK theme and draws on the areas of knowledge the course covers. Choosing the theme is what narrows the field of objects from everything to something a student can argue about in 950 words, so this is where a first session usually goes.

subjects.name: Knowledge and the knower (core theme)
subjects.description: The core theme asks how the knower's own position shapes what they accept as knowledge. Most exhibitions sit here because the objects can be personal: a document, a family possession, a school report. The risk is the opposite of generic — commentaries drift into autobiography and stop analysing the prompt.

subjects.name: Knowledge and technology (optional theme)
subjects.description: The most popular optional theme in UAE classrooms, partly because digital objects are easy to source and timestamp. A specific post, a recommendation feed, a dataset or a piece of software all qualify. Students who choose this theme must resist making the commentary a general argument about social media.

subjects.name: Knowledge and language (optional theme)
subjects.description: Strong ground in a country where most students work in English and live in Arabic, Hindi, Malayalam, Tagalog or Russian. Translated documents, bilingual signage and untranslatable terms make excellent objects because the real-world context is immediate and the knowledge claim is visible in the object itself.

subjects.name: Knowledge and politics (optional theme)
subjects.description: Powerful but demanding. Objects need to be specific artefacts — a named treaty page, a ballot, a published figure — and the commentary must analyse how knowledge is produced and contested rather than taking a political position. Teachers in the UAE usually steer students towards documents and data over contemporary controversy.

subjects.name: Knowledge and religion (optional theme)
subjects.description: Chosen less often, and handled carefully. The task is epistemological: how religious knowledge is justified, transmitted and interpreted. The commentary analyses the processes around an object rather than evaluating belief. Students taking Islamic Education alongside the diploma often have unusually good material here.

subjects.name: Knowledge and indigenous societies (optional theme)
subjects.description: The least-used theme and therefore the least generic. Objects tied to transmitted, place-based knowledge work well, and UAE students have genuine access to them through heritage collections and oral tradition. Research load is higher, so this theme suits a student who starts early.

subjects.name: The natural sciences (area of knowledge)
subjects.description: Supplies objects about method, measurement and replication: an instrument, a retracted paper, a calibration certificate. Science students often pick these and then write about the science instead of the knowledge question, which is the single most common way a promising object produces a middle-band commentary.

subjects.name: The human sciences (area of knowledge)
subjects.description: Census forms, survey instruments and published indicators make precise objects with datable contexts. The strength of this AOK for the exhibition is that the object usually embodies a methodological choice, and a methodological choice is exactly what an IA prompt about evidence or certainty wants examined.

subjects.name: Mathematics (area of knowledge)
subjects.description: Harder to object-ify and therefore distinctive when done well: a proof as printed in a named edition, a geometric pattern on a specific building, an abacus with a provenance. Students must avoid turning the commentary into mathematics; the assessment is about how mathematical knowledge is justified.

subjects.name: History (area of knowledge)
subjects.description: The most reliable source of good exhibition objects because every historical artefact arrives with a date, a place and a chain of custody. UAE students have strong local material, from pearling-era implements to founding-era documents, and local material is by definition not what every other candidate has chosen.

subjects.name: The arts (area of knowledge)
subjects.description: Specific works, not genres. A named painting in a named collection, a particular recording, one photograph. The frequent error is choosing a famous work whose context is so well rehearsed that the commentary cannot say anything a marker has not read twenty times.

subjects.name: TOK essay planning (DP2 follow-on)
subjects.description: Not part of the exhibition, but the reason families keep a TOK slot after upload. The essay responds to one of six prescribed titles, runs to a published word ceiling, and is marked outside the school. Families who plan TOK essay and exhibition planning together avoid rebuilding the habit from scratch a year later.

ib-tok-exhibition-help.regionsTitle: Where your child's school sits, and who sets the date there
ib-tok-exhibition-help.regionsIntro: The exhibition deadline is always set inside the school, but the regulator above the school decides how fees, calendars and mandatory subjects are approved, and that shapes which weeks are actually available for the work. Here is the practical position across the seven emirates.

regions.name: Dubai
regions.note: The largest DP cohort in the country and the tightest term calendar. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in every private school alongside the licensed curriculum, so a DP1 week already carries lessons that do not count towards the diploma. Exhibition work has to fit around them.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi
regions.note: ADEK supervises licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. DP cohorts here are smaller per school and TOK is often taught by a single teacher, which means one person reads every commentary. IB DP1 TOK support in Abu Dhabi usually works best booked around the school's own draft-feedback date.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Also under ADEK, with fewer IB World Schools and longer school-run distances. Families here feel the travel argument most sharply: a visiting tutor prices the drive into the hour, while a live video session costs the same at 8pm as at 4pm and does not depend on who happens to live nearby.

regions.name: Sharjah
regions.note: The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in the emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. TOK exhibition help for Sharjah students is frequently booked late because the exhibition is taught in a term already carrying heavy coursework from other subjects.

regions.name: Ajman
regions.note: Private schools here are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education. IB provision is limited, so some Ajman families have a child at a Dubai or Sharjah school with a commute of an hour each way. That commute is the reason an online slot at 7.30pm is often the only realistic session time.

regions.name: Ras Al Khaimah
regions.note: Regulated by the emirate's Department of Knowledge, which also approves curricula and assessment methods. Distance from the Dubai tutoring market is absolute for an in-home visit and irrelevant for a video lesson, which is why northern-emirates families are among the clearest beneficiaries of online delivery.

regions.name: Fujairah
regions.note: Under the federal Ministry of Education. East-coast families typically have the fewest local options for a subject as narrow as Theory of Knowledge, and the exhibition is narrower still. Matching on specialism rather than postcode is the whole point of the model.

regions.name: Umm Al Quwain
regions.note: Also supervised by the Ministry of Education, and the smallest private-school market in the country. Where no local tutor teaches TOK at all, we say so before you book rather than after, and the free trial lesson is where that gets established.

ib-tok-exhibition-help.modesIntro: Exhibition work has a shape: a research phase, a choosing phase, a writing phase and a review phase. The format that suits it changes as the deadline approaches, so most families use more than one of the four below across a single term.

modes.description: A single 60-minute session, usually booked eight to ten weeks out, that ends with a shortlist of candidate objects and one IA prompt the student can defend. The student does the choosing; the tutor's job is to ask why each object is that object and not a category, and to stop a weak shortlist from consuming a whole term.

sections.heading: What a UAE parent is actually asking for when they search for TOK exhibition help
paragraphs: The search is almost always triggered by a specific message from school, and the question underneath it is narrow: what exactly has my child been asked to produce, and is what they have produced any good? The answer is that the TOK exhibition is a single document plus three images. Your child chooses three objects, links all three to one IA prompt from the thirty-five the IB publishes, and writes a commentary of no more than 950 words that identifies each object, places it in a specific real-world context, and justifies why it answers that prompt.

Three details catch families out. The first is that all three objects share one prompt — students who pick a different prompt for each object have misread the task and usually have to restart. The second is that the objects must be particular things, not kinds of thing: a specific passport issued to a specific person on a specific date, not "passports". The third is that the commentary is not an essay with an introduction and a conclusion. It is three justifications, written tightly enough that 950 words is comfortable rather than crushing.

What support looks like, then, is not content delivery. There is no syllabus to teach through. It is a sequence of questions that force specificity: whose object is this, when did it enter the world, what happened to it, what knowledge claim does its existence support, and what would count as evidence for the link you are asserting? A student who can answer those five questions about each of three objects has a strong commentary available to them. A student who cannot has a middle-band commentary no amount of editing will rescue.

The table below sets out the task element by element, with the error each element reliably produces and what a session actually does about it. It is the version of the task most UAE schools communicate in a single slide, expanded into the detail parents ask for afterwards.

sections.heading: The thirty-five IA prompts, grouped so a DP1 student can choose one in an afternoon
paragraphs: The IB publishes a fixed list of thirty-five IA prompts and students must use one of them unaltered. We do not reproduce the list here — it belongs to the IB and lives in the current TOK guide your child's teacher will have issued. What is useful is a map of the families the prompts fall into, because a student who knows which family they want can scan the official list in minutes instead of reading all thirty-five as if they were interchangeable.

Broadly, the prompts cluster around six concerns. There are prompts about evidence and what counts as adequate justification. There are prompts about certainty, doubt and the limits of what can be known. There are prompts about method and the tools knowledge is produced with. There are prompts about the knower's perspective, position and bias. There are prompts about values, ethics and responsibility in knowledge production. And there are prompts about change: how knowledge is replaced, revised, or quietly abandoned.

The choosing order matters more than the choice. Students who pick a prompt first and then hunt for objects to fit it almost always end up with one strong object and two forced ones. Students who assemble six or seven objects they genuinely know something about, and then ask which prompt all three of a subset could honestly serve, end up with a commentary that writes itself. The prompt is a lens, and lenses are chosen after you know what you want to look at.

One practical constraint: the prompt has to be answerable three times without repetition. If two of the three justifications would say the same thing in different words, the commentary will read as thin even if each object is well chosen. Testing for that in week eight is a twenty-minute job. Discovering it in week two of a three-week writing phase means starting the selection again with no time left.

sections.heading: Choosing three objects that can carry a 950-word commentary
paragraphs: Object selection is where the exhibition is won or lost, and it is the part of the task a tutor can help with most legitimately and most carefully. The student must choose; that selection is assessed. What a session does is interrogate candidates — and interrogation is teaching, not substitution. The test applied to every candidate object is the same: can you tell me, in three sentences, what this thing is, when and where it existed, and who had it?

Objects that pass that test share a property. They are instances, not classes. A grandparent's identity document issued in a named year passes. "Identity documents" does not. A specific recording of a specific performance passes. "Classical music" does not. Digital objects are explicitly acceptable and often excellent, because a post, a dataset or a software release carries a timestamp and a URL — the provenance is built in. What disqualifies an object is not its subject matter but the absence of a single real-world context to describe.

The second filter is distinctiveness. Nothing in the assessment rewards obscurity, but a commentary about a famous object has to work harder, because the marker has read the standard account of it many times. UAE students have an advantage here that they consistently fail to use: local material. Pearling-era implements, founding-era documents, a bilingual street sign, a school's own first enrolment register, a family's migration papers. These are objects with verifiable contexts that no other candidate in the cohort has chosen.

The last filter is practical. Each object needs an image the student can legitimately include, and a context they can check rather than assume. An object in a museum the student has visited is easier than one they have only read about. The table below is the triage we run on a shortlist in the first consultation.

sections.heading: The exhibition counted backwards from your school's upload date
paragraphs: Ask the school one question before you plan anything: what is the internal date by which the commentary must be with the TOK teacher? That date, not the IB's submission window, is the one your child has to meet, and in most UAE schools it sits between three and eight weeks earlier. Schools that read a draft before the internal date have a second, earlier deadline that matters just as much, and it is frequently communicated once, verbally, in a lesson.

With that date fixed, the work divides cleanly. Weeks ten to eight are research and shortlisting, and they are the weeks families skip. Weeks seven to five are selection and justification, done out loud before anything is drafted. Weeks four to two are writing, with a word budget per object agreed in advance. The final fortnight is review against the instrument and the mechanical checks — images, citations, file format, the school's submission platform. None of this requires more than one hour a week until the writing phase.

The counting-backwards habit also protects against the specific UAE problem of a term that is not as long as it looks. Between a winter break, National Day, an Eid holiday whose dates move, and the internal assessment calendar of six other subjects, a notional ten-week run frequently contains seven working weeks. A plan built on calendar weeks fails. A plan built on sessions and deliverables survives, because a missing week pushes a deliverable rather than collapsing the task.

The table is the version we work to. The last column is deliberately explicit about the limits of what a tutor may do, because on an internally assessed component those limits are the difference between support and malpractice.

sections.heading: Where the ten marks go, and what moves a commentary up a band
paragraphs: The exhibition is marked out of ten against a single global assessment instrument with five bands, by the school's own TOK teacher, and the school's marks are then externally moderated by the IB. There are no separate criteria letters to collect, which surprises families who have come through subject Internal Assessments with their lettered criteria and per-criterion mark allocations. One instrument, applied to the whole commentary, is the entire mechanism.

What the instrument rewards is not writing quality. It is whether all three objects are clearly identified, whether each is placed in a specific real-world context, and whether the link to the IA prompt is justified with explicit evidence. A commentary can be elegant and still sit in the middle bands because its links are asserted rather than argued. A plainer commentary that names its evidence for each of three links reads much higher, and this is the single most actionable thing a DP1 student can be told.

The diagnostic shortcut is to read each object's paragraph and ask: which sentence here is the justification? If the answer is "all of it" or "none of it", the paragraph is describing. A justification is identifiable — it contains a because, a therefore, or an appeal to something checkable. Students who learn to point at their own justification sentence stop producing the middle-band commentary almost immediately, because they can see the gap themselves.

sections.heading: How the exhibition sits inside the TOK grade and the diploma
paragraphs: The exhibition carries one third of the TOK grade. The TOK essay, written in DP2 against one of six prescribed titles released by the IB and marked by an examiner outside the school, carries the other two thirds. The two components produce a single letter from A to E. That letter is then read together with the Extended Essay grade to award up to three points on top of the six subject grades, using a matrix the IB publishes.

The consequence families need to understand early is asymmetric. A strong exhibition does not guarantee a strong TOK grade, because the externally marked essay weighs twice as much. But a weak exhibition is very hard to recover from, because the only remaining component is the one your child has least control over — a title they did not write, marked by someone who has never met them. The exhibition is the part of TOK where effort converts most directly into grade.

There is also a failing condition. A grade E in Theory of Knowledge or in the Extended Essay prevents the award of the diploma regardless of subject points. This is the reason a DP1 student who treats TOK as the course that can be ignored until it matters is taking a risk out of proportion to the time involved. An hour a week through one term is a small insurance premium against the only component that can void an otherwise good diploma.

sections.heading: Academic honesty on an internally assessed component: the line, and who draws it
paragraphs: The exhibition is marked inside the school, which makes the honesty question sharper than it is for an exam. Your child signs that the work is their own, the teacher authenticates it, and the IB moderates the result. A commentary containing sentences the student did not compose is a malpractice finding, and the consequence falls on the student rather than on whoever supplied the sentences. That asymmetry is why every tutoring arrangement for this component should have an explicit boundary.

Ours is simple and we state it on the page because the alternative is parents guessing. A tutor may ask questions, explain what a requirement means, challenge a weak justification, point at a paragraph and say which requirement it fails to meet, and confirm mechanical matters like word count and citation format. A tutor may not select objects for the student, supply justifications, compose or rewrite commentary text, or hand over a model commentary to work from. Any provider offering to supply finished assessed work is selling the student a malpractice risk.

Generative AI sits in the same frame. Unattributed machine-written text in a commentary is not a style problem; it is undisclosed authorship, and the IB and your child's school both have policies on it. The school's policy is the one that applies, and it is worth reading before the writing phase rather than during it. Using a tool to find candidate objects and then verifying each one independently is a different activity from having a tool produce the justification.

The school's own rules take precedence over anything on this page. If your child's TOK teacher sets a narrower limit on outside feedback than the IB's general position, that narrower limit is the operative one and we work inside it.

sections.heading: Who regulates your child's school, and what you can ask it for
paragraphs: No UAE regulator sets the exhibition deadline. That is worth saying plainly, because parents sometimes look for the date in the wrong place. The IB sets the submission window for schools; the school sets the internal date for students. What the emirate regulator governs is the licensing of the school, the approval of its fees and, in several emirates, the approval of curricula and assessment methods — the frame inside which the school's calendar is built.

The map is fixed and worth knowing. In Dubai, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. In Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, the Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools. In Sharjah, the Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge holds the same role, and the federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

Two things follow for a family planning exhibition support. First, nobody outside the school can tell you the date, so ask the school directly and ask for both dates — the internal submission date and any earlier draft-feedback date. Second, be sceptical of any tutoring provider describing itself in terms of a regulator. A permit to operate a training institute with premises in Dubai is a specific thing issued to specific organisations; it is not a quality badge that attaches to online one-to-one tuition, and IB Gram does not claim it.

On the tutor side there is a real and checkable requirement. Individuals providing private lessons in the UAE need a private tuition work permit, introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tutoring without a permit is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted figure with suspicion.

sections.heading: Ramadan, National Day and the ministry subjects sharing the same term
paragraphs: A UAE exhibition term is shorter than it looks on paper, and the reasons are local. Winter break, Commemoration Day and National Day in early December, an Eid holiday whose dates shift year to year, and in some years Ramadan falling across the second half of the term all remove working weeks from a plan that assumed them. A ten-week run on the calendar is routinely seven or eight weeks of actual work, and the weeks that get eaten are the research weeks at the front.

Ramadan changes the shape of the week rather than removing it. School hours shorten, the productive part of the evening moves after Iftar, and a 4pm session that worked in November is the worst possible slot in March. Online delivery handles this without negotiation: a post-Iftar slot costs the same as an afternoon one and requires nobody to drive anywhere at the end of a fasting day. Families who tell us in February which weeks Ramadan will affect keep their cadence; families who tell us in week one of Ramadan lose a fortnight.

The other squeeze is structural and specific to this country. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with KHDA requiring the arrangements to be in place from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, advises that no mandatory lesson run shorter than 25 minutes, and requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited.

For a DP1 student that means several periods a week that carry real assessment weight at school and contribute nothing to the diploma score. It is one of the honest reasons a diploma student in Dubai has less discretionary time than the raw timetable suggests, and it is why exhibition planning that ignores the school week fails. Put the ministry subjects, the mock calendar and the holidays on one page before deciding which weeks the exhibition actually gets.

sections.heading: What TOK exhibition support costs across the UAE market
paragraphs: Three of the six most visible providers in this market publish no price at all, and two of those that do quote in US dollars — a currency UAE families do not transact in. So here is what the market actually charges in dirhams, taken from providers' own published pages read in October 2026 and from Bestimate's Dubai 2026 tutoring rate table. These are market figures attributed to their sources. They are not IB Gram's price list, and nothing on this page should be read as a quote.

The pattern across the bands is consistent. Budget online tuition starts around AED 33 to 65 an hour and is almost never staffed by anyone who has taught Theory of Knowledge, because TOK is a narrow teaching speciality rather than a subject every tutor has covered. Qualified subject tutors online sit roughly AED 150 to 300. IB specialists run about AED 200 to 450 and above. Visiting in-home tutors run AED 180 to 500, and a meaningful part of that spread is the travel priced into the hour. Premium named tutors reach AED 650.

Coursework supervision is the gap. No UAE provider in our October 2026 research published a rate for a defined block of Extended Essay or TOK supervision, which is exactly the shape exhibition support takes — five to eight sessions across one term, not an open-ended weekly commitment. We quote after a free trial lesson instead of publishing a number that would be wrong for half the families reading it, and the trial requires no card details and no commitment to a block afterwards.

One piece of context worth holding alongside the rates: KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for Dubai private schools for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package. For a family budgeting a DP1 year, a fee freeze plus a one-term exhibition block is a very different calculation from a fee rise plus two years of weekly tuition.

sections.heading: Why a document task is better served live online than by a visiting tutor
paragraphs: The honest comparison here is not about which format is nicer. It is about what the session physically has to do. Exhibition support means reading a specific draft, pointing at a specific paragraph, and asking the student to justify a specific link. That work happens on a document. A shared screen with the draft open and both people looking at the same sentence is the native format for it, and a printed copy across a table is a worse version of the same thing.

The second factor is who is available. Theory of Knowledge is taught by a small subset of DP teachers, and the exhibition specifically by a smaller subset still. Matching on proximity means choosing from whoever lives within a reasonable drive of your community. Matching online means choosing a TOK specialist and ignoring geography entirely. For a family in Fujairah, Umm Al Quwain or Ras Al Khaimah, that is not a marginal improvement; it is the difference between a specialist and nobody.

Third, session economics. A visiting tutor who drives 40 minutes each way needs a long booking to make the trip worthwhile, which pushes families towards two-hour sessions. A 950-word commentary does not need two hours. It needs forty-five focused minutes on one criterion, repeated. Short and frequent beats long and occasional on a task this size, and only one format makes short and frequent affordable.

To be completely clear about what we sell: IB Gram delivers UAE tuition as one-to-one lessons over live video, and home visits are a service we offer only in India. We say so before you book rather than after. The free trial lesson exists so you can judge the format on the actual work — bring the current draft, or the shortlist of objects, and see what a session does with it.

sections.heading: After upload: the essay term, and the equivalency file nobody opens early
paragraphs: Once the commentary is submitted, two clocks start. The first is the TOK essay, which belongs to DP2 and responds to one of six prescribed titles released by the IB for each session. It is marked by an examiner outside the school and it is two thirds of the TOK grade, so a family that has just built a working habit around the exhibition should spend one session converting that habit into an essay timeline rather than letting it lapse for eight months.

The second clock is the one almost nobody starts in DP1: Ministry of Education equivalency. Equivalency is the process by which a UAE authority recognises a school-leaving certificate for local university entry and other official purposes. It is a regulatory process, not a tutoring one — we describe it, point you at the official channel, and nothing more. It is also not something tutoring is required for, and any provider implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency around a government procedure.

The sourced detail matters because at least one ranking competitor publishes it wrongly. On the British track, students must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. On the American track, English proficiency requires a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the SAT reading and writing section, and mathematics requires at least 450 in SAT Math.

For the IB there is no figure on this page, and that is deliberate. The source we read publishes no IB points threshold, and we will not print one that has not been read on the ministry's own site. Ask your DP coordinator and verify on moe.gov.ae before you plan around any number you find on a tutoring page, including a number you find on a page that looks more confident than this one.

process.title: Tell us the date, not just the subject
process.description: The first message we need is the school's internal submission date and any earlier draft-feedback date. Everything else — how many sessions, which weeks, what each session does — is derived from those two dates. A family that supplies them gets a plan in the first reply instead of a generic package.

process.title: A free trial lesson on the actual work
process.description: One session at no charge, with no card details taken and no obligation to book a block afterwards. Bring the shortlist of objects or the current draft. Forty-five minutes is usually enough to see whether the questions being asked are moving the work or just filling the hour.

process.title: Match on specialism, with coverage stated honestly
process.description: We look for a tutor who has taught Theory of Knowledge, not a subject teacher willing to try. Where no specialist is free in the window your deadline needs, we say so before you book and tell you what is available instead. Concealing a coverage gap costs more than admitting one.

process.title: Work the countdown, one deliverable per block
process.description: Sessions follow the backwards plan: shortlist, then selection, then provenance notes, then the student's own draft, then review against the instrument. Each block ends with something that exists. Nothing is marked as progress unless it is written down somewhere your child can show the teacher.

process.title: Hand back to the school, and plan the essay term
process.description: The teacher's feedback always takes priority over ours, and in the final fortnight we work inside it rather than alongside it. After upload, one session converts the exhibition habit into a DP2 essay timeline so the same scramble does not repeat with higher stakes.

whyPoints.title: Built around a deadline, not a package
whyPoints.description: Exhibition support has a natural end: the upload date. We plan to it and stop, rather than selling an open-ended weekly commitment. Families who need something after that come back for the essay term because they chose to, not because a subscription rolled over.

whyPoints.title: The boundary is written down
whyPoints.description: What a tutor may and may not do on an internally assessed component is set out on this page in a table, before you book. On a component your child signs for and the school authenticates, an explicit limit protects the student far better than an unstated assumption about good intentions.

whyPoints.title: TOK specialists, not subject teachers improvising
whyPoints.description: Theory of Knowledge is a distinct course with a distinct assessment, and the exhibition is its least familiar component. We match on having taught it. Where we cannot, we say so rather than putting a capable physics teacher in front of an IA prompt they have never used.

whyPoints.title: Figures that carry their source and date
whyPoints.description: Every AED band on this page names the provider or table it came from and the month it was read. Three of the most visible providers in this market publish no price at all. Showing the method is how a parent can check a number instead of taking it on trust.

whyPoints.title: Scheduled for a UAE week
whyPoints.description: Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time, after school, after work or post-Iftar during Ramadan, and the slot moves when the school calendar moves. The ministry subjects, mock weeks and December holidays go into the plan at the start rather than being discovered as it collapses.

whyPoints.title: No promises about a mark
whyPoints.description: Nobody can honestly guarantee a band on a ten-mark instrument marked inside a school and moderated by the IB. What a tutor can change is whether three objects are instances, whether each link has evidence, and whether the draft exists before the final week.

faqs.question: How many objects does the TOK exhibition need, and can two of them use different IA prompts?
faqs.answer: Three objects, and they all share one IA prompt. This is the most common misreading of the task we see in a first session: students pick three interesting objects, find a different prompt that suits each, and produce a commentary that cannot be marked as intended. The three objects are three answers to the same question. If two of your child's objects would answer a prompt in near-identical terms, swap one before the writing phase begins, because a commentary with two overlapping justifications reads as thin however well each is written.

faqs.question: What actually counts as an object for the exhibition?
faqs.answer: A particular thing with a real-world context that can be described and checked — one passport issued to one person on one date, one recording of one performance, one post from one named account at a named time. Digital objects are acceptable and often ideal, because the timestamp and source are built in. What fails is a class of thing: a telescope, a map, a smartphone. There is no single context to analyse, so the commentary ends up describing a category. The working test is whether your child can say what it is, when and where it existed, and who had it.

faqs.question: Which of the thirty-five IA prompts should my child choose first?
faqs.answer: None of them, first. Choose objects first. Students who pick a prompt and then hunt for objects to fit it typically end up with one strong object and two forced ones, because the prompt has become a constraint rather than a lens. The better order is to assemble six or seven objects your child genuinely knows something about, then ask which single prompt three of them could honestly serve. The prompts cluster into families — evidence, certainty, method, perspective, values, and change over time — so once your child knows which family fits their objects, the official list takes minutes to scan.

faqs.question: Does the 950-word ceiling include the object descriptions and the citations?
faqs.answer: Treat 950 words as the ceiling for the commentary itself and confirm the current counting rules with your child's TOK teacher, because the school applies the IB's guidance and submits through its own platform. The practical advice is independent of the detail: budget the words per object before drafting rather than cutting afterwards. Students who write 1,400 words and then cut almost always cut justification, which is the part the assessment instrument rewards, and keep description, which it does not. A planned budget of roughly 300 words per object plus a short framing passage leaves no painful decisions in the last week.

faqs.question: When in DP1 do UAE schools usually set the exhibition deadline?
faqs.answer: Earlier than families expect. Many UAE schools finish the exhibition before the DP1 summer, because the second year is crowded with Internal Assessments, the Extended Essay and mocks. The date is set inside the school, not by the IB and not by any emirate regulator, so the only reliable answer comes from your child's TOK teacher or DP coordinator. Ask for two dates rather than one: the internal submission date, and any earlier date by which a draft will be read. The second one is often mentioned once in a lesson and never written down.

faqs.question: My child's three objects are all taken from recent news. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, but it carries two risks worth checking. The first is specificity: a news story is not an object, though a particular published article, photograph or dataset is. The second is distinctiveness. If a story is prominent enough that several candidates in the same cohort have reached for it, the commentary has to work harder to say something a marker has not already read. Local material usually solves both problems at once — a family document, a bilingual sign, a heritage artefact in a collection your child has visited. Verifiable, specific, and almost certainly nobody else's choice.

faqs.question: How is the exhibition marked, and does anyone outside the school see it?
faqs.answer: It is marked out of ten by your child's own TOK teacher against a single global assessment instrument with five bands, and the school's marks are then externally moderated by the IB. There are no separate criteria letters to collect as there are in subject Internal Assessments. Moderation matters because it means the school's judgement is checked rather than final — a cohort marked generously or harshly can be adjusted. For a parent, the useful consequence is that the instrument's requirements, not a teacher's preferences, are what the work should be read against.

faqs.question: Can a tutor suggest objects for my child's exhibition?
faqs.answer: A tutor can question a shortlist your child has produced; a tutor cannot produce the shortlist. The selection is part of what is assessed, so handing over a list of objects substitutes someone else's thinking for the student's and puts the student at risk on a component they have to authenticate. What a session legitimately does is apply pressure: why this object and not the category it belongs to, what is its real-world context, what evidence supports the link you are claiming. That pressure usually eliminates two or three weak candidates in twenty minutes without anyone supplying anything.

faqs.question: The commentary has come back 300 words over, two days before upload. What now?
faqs.answer: Cut description, never justification. Read each object's paragraph and find the sentence that does the justifying — the one with a because or an appeal to something checkable. Protect those. Everything that explains what the object is, rather than where it sits and why it answers the prompt, is a candidate for compression. Framing passages are usually the next cut; students often write an essay-style opening the task does not require. If your child cannot locate a justification sentence in a paragraph, the word count is not actually the problem and the overrun is a symptom.

faqs.question: Is the exhibition displayed to an audience, or is it just a document submitted online?
faqs.answer: Schools vary. The assessed artefact is the commentary plus images of the three objects, submitted through the school, and that is what is marked and moderated. Many schools also run an internal showcase where students present their objects to peers, parents or younger year groups — valuable for the student, but not what the mark comes from. If your child's school runs one, treat it as rehearsal: explaining three objects out loud to a stranger is the fastest way to discover which justification does not hold up.

faqs.question: How many sessions does exhibition support usually take?
faqs.answer: Between five and eight across one term, in our experience of this component, which is why we treat it as a defined block rather than an open weekly commitment. One session on theme and shortlist, one or two on selection and testing the prompt, one on provenance notes, then two or three reviewing the student's own draft against the instrument. Families who start ten weeks out tend towards the lower number because nothing has to be redone. Families who arrive with three weeks left often need more sessions for a worse result, because selection errors cannot be edited away.

faqs.question: What does TOK exhibition support cost across the UAE market?
faqs.answer: Market rates in the UAE for IB specialist tuition run roughly AED 200 to 450 an hour and above, with budget online tuition from about AED 33 to 65, qualified online subject tutors around AED 150 to 300, visiting in-home tutors AED 180 to 500, and premium named tutors reaching AED 650 — figures published by EdFlik, Tutopiya, Unitors, TutorChase, BartyED and Bestimate's Dubai 2026 table, read October 2026. No provider we surveyed publishes a rate for a defined coursework supervision block. We quote after a free trial lesson, which takes no card details and carries no obligation to book.

faqs.question: Can my child use an AI tool to find objects or tidy up the commentary?
faqs.answer: Your child's school policy is the operative rule and should be read before the writing phase, not during it. The distinction that matters is authorship. Using a tool to surface candidate objects and then independently verifying each one's context is research. Having a tool produce or rewrite commentary text is undisclosed authorship, and on a component the student signs for and the teacher authenticates, that is a malpractice finding rather than a style issue. The safe position is that every sentence submitted was composed by the student, and anything else is disclosed exactly as the school requires.

faqs.question: We are in Sharjah and the school has not mentioned the exhibition yet. Should we chase it?
faqs.answer: Ask, politely and early. The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in the emirate and approves curricula and assessment methods, but it does not set your child's exhibition date — the school does. A single email to the DP coordinator asking for the internal submission date and the draft-feedback date costs nothing and converts the whole term from reactive to planned. In our experience the information usually exists and has simply been communicated once, verbally, to a class in which your child was not taking notes.

faqs.question: Does the exhibition mark affect the Ministry of Education equivalency file?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Equivalency recognises the completed certificate, not individual components, and it is a regulatory process run by the ministry rather than anything a tutoring provider performs or influences. The sourced British-track requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one A-Level at E or two AS-Levels. For the IB, the source we read publishes no points threshold, so verify on moe.gov.ae or with your DP coordinator and ignore any figure a tutoring site states confidently without a ministry citation.

faqs.question: Does Ramadan move the exhibition deadline, and what happens to our weekly session?
faqs.answer: The deadline is the school's and it rarely moves, so the session has to. School hours shorten during Ramadan and the productive part of the evening sits after Iftar, which makes a 4pm slot that worked in November the worst available option in March. Because lessons run over live video, a post-Iftar slot costs the same as an afternoon one and nobody drives anywhere at the end of a fasting day. Tell us in February which weeks will be affected and the cadence holds; tell us in the first week of Ramadan and a fortnight is usually lost.

ib-tok-exhibition-help.closingHeading: Start by asking the school for two dates
ib-tok-exhibition-help.closingBody: Everything useful about IB TOK exhibition help in the UAE follows from the internal submission date and the draft-feedback date your child's school has already set. Send us those two dates and we will come back with a week-by-week plan, including what each session delivers and roughly how many your child's remaining time allows. A free trial lesson comes first, with no card details and no obligation to book a block afterwards — bring the shortlist of objects or the draft as it stands. Lessons run one to one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; home visits are a service we offer only in India, and we say so before you book rather than after.

intro.heading: The system your child's Diploma sits inside
paragraphs: IB tuition in the UAE means one-to-one teaching in a named IB subject, delivered over live video and scheduled around a Gulf school week. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address: every lesson runs online, one student and one specialist, with a free trial lesson before you commit. That delivery decision is the first thing to say plainly, because the rest of this page is about the system the lessons have to work inside, and the system is the part no competing page describes.

Start with the arithmetic of the market you are shopping in. Dubai's private sector held 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula, split 37% UK curriculum, 26% Indian, 14% American and 7% International Baccalaureate, according to the Dubai Media Office. Seven in a hundred. When a local agency says it covers everything, the arithmetic says its bench is built for the 37% and the 26%. That is why an IB parent so often ends up with a tutor who knows the content but not the assessment model, and why a Chemistry grade can stay flat through a term of paid help.

Then there is the regulatory map, which matters more here than almost anywhere else because families move. Dubai's schools answer to the Knowledge and Human Development Authority. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain answer to the Department of Education and Knowledge. Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah sit with the federal Ministry of Education, per the government's own u.ae guidance. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so a cross-emirate move is not only a change of commute.

Movement is the defining feature of this market and the thing tuition is most often bought to repair. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened in 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6%, KHDA reported. New places mean transfers, and transfers mean students joining a Diploma cohort after the first Internal Assessment has been set, or arriving from an IGCSE, CBSE or American programme into a course that assumes two years of a particular way of thinking.

So this page answers the questions the system actually generates: who licenses and approves what, what breaks when a family changes school or emirate mid-programme, which Arabic and Islamic Education class your child is placed in and why that is not negotiable, who is legally permitted to tutor in the UAE, what the market charges in AED, what the Ministry counts towards equivalency, and where an extra weekly hour fits in a term that already contains a shortened Ramadan timetable. Nothing on it is a promise about a grade.

ib-tuition.programmesIntro: The IB is four programmes, not one, and UAE schools license them in different combinations: a Dubai school may run the Primary Years Programme and then hand students to an IGCSE Middle Years stream, while another runs the continuum end to end. Which combination your school holds changes what tuition is for.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is inquiry-led and has no external examination, which makes it the programme parents find hardest to read. Progress appears as teacher judgements against learning outcomes rather than as marks out of a hundred, so a parent asking whether a child is behind often cannot tell from the report alone. Tuition at this stage is diagnostic: reading fluency, number sense, written structure, and the English a transition into a Middle Years stream will assume.
programmes.countryNote: In the UAE the PYP runs alongside mandatory Ministry subjects from the earliest grades, and in Dubai those subjects follow KHDA's own requirements regardless of the school's licensed curriculum. A PYP child in a Dubai school is therefore timetabled for Arabic and for Moral, Social and Cultural Studies or Social Studies depending on placement, and those subjects appear on the school report beside the inquiry units.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP assesses against four criteria per subject, each scored on an eight-point band, and converts those bands into a one-to-seven grade. Families who arrive from a percentage system misread this constantly: a strong piece of work scoring six on one criterion and three on another produces a mid grade that looks like generalised weakness when it is a single specific gap. Tuition works best here when it targets one criterion at a time.
programmes.countryNote: Many UAE schools run the MYP only to Year 9 or Year 10 and then switch students into IGCSE for the final two years, because an IGCSE certificate is a document the Ministry of Education's equivalency route recognises directly. If that is your school's pattern, the useful question is which of the five accredited subjects your child is on track to pass, not how the MYP grade looks in isolation.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma is six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Marks come from externally examined papers and from internally assessed work that the school marks and the IB moderates. The load is front-ended with coursework and back-ended with examinations, so a student can look comfortable in the first year and be a long way behind by the second.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools sit the May session, and the practical consequence is that the Diploma's internal deadlines land in a UAE school year that includes a shortened Ramadan timetable and a long summer break between the two years. Confirm your own session and results dates with the school's IB coordinator or on ibo.org; this page does not publish IB dates, because the IB's own site could not be verified when it was written.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: The Career-related Programme pairs at least two Diploma courses with a career-related study, a reflective project, a service-learning element and a personal and professional skills course. It is a genuine IB route rather than a consolation one, and a student who would be stretched thin across six Diploma subjects can do considerably better on two or three taught properly. Tuition focuses on those Diploma courses and on the reflective project's process.
programmes.countryNote: The CP is licensed by far fewer UAE schools than the Diploma, so a family drawn to it may be weighing a school transfer to reach one. Before moving, check what the receiving school's licence actually covers with its registrar and check how the resulting certificate maps to the university route you have in mind, because a Career-related Programme certificate is a different document from a Diploma in an equivalency file.

ib-tuition.subjectsIntro: Subject choice in the UAE is often made under a constraint: a school with one Physics teacher at Higher Level, a timetable block that forces a choice between Economics and a second science, or a transfer that lands mid-course. These are the subjects UAE families most often ask for, with the part of each where marks actually move.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The route most engineering and economics courses expect. Marks are lost in proof, in calculus technique under time pressure, and in the exploration, where a student picks a topic too large to treat properly. Students arriving from IGCSE Extended maths usually have the algebra and not the formal reasoning.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and technology-heavy work, with a graphical display calculator paper that rewards fluency in the tool itself. Weak marks here are rarely about mathematics: they are about reading a long modelling question, choosing the right test, and writing a conclusion that references the data rather than the hope.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The syllabus rewards precision in moles, equilibria and energetics, and punishes vague language in extended response. The internally assessed scientific investigation carries its own criteria and its own common failure: a research question that cannot be answered with the data the student can realistically collect.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics and fields reward a student who draws the situation before writing an equation. Where UAE students most often lose marks is in uncertainty and error treatment in the investigation, and in multi-step questions where the first line of working is right and the chain breaks at the substitution.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume makes this the subject where revision method matters more than hours. Command terms separate the grades: outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each want a different shape of answer, and a student who writes everything they know for every verb loses marks they have already earned in their head.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Often chosen to satisfy two groups at once, and often underestimated. It demands systems language, case studies with real places and numbers, and an evaluative register. UAE students have strong local material available to them in water, energy and food security, and the ones who use it specifically read far better than the ones who write in generalities.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams are the grade. A correctly labelled diagram, explained in a sentence that refers to the axes, earns marks that prose alone will not. The internally assessed commentaries fail on article choice more than on analysis: an article with no clear economic event in it cannot carry a strong commentary.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools are easy to recall and hard to apply. Students lose marks by describing a framework instead of using it on the named organisation, and by writing conclusions that do not answer the question asked. Case-study discipline, taught deliberately, moves this grade faster than content revision does.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A UAE cohort typically contains strong readers writing in a second or third language. The gap is usually structural rather than linguistic: paragraphs that describe rather than analyse, and a thesis that restates the question. Timed writing practice with specific feedback on one paragraph at a time is what changes the mark.

subjects.name: Arabic B and Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: Chosen both by students continuing from school Arabic and by those starting the language inside the Diploma. Marks turn on text-type conventions and on productive vocabulary under timed conditions rather than on reading comprehension, which is usually the stronger half of a UAE student's profile.

subjects.name: French B and Spanish ab initio
subjects.description: The second-language options UAE schools most commonly offer beside Arabic. The individual oral is where confident students underperform, because it rewards rehearsed structures and a clear position on the stimulus rather than fluency on its own. Weekly spoken practice with correction is the single highest-return intervention.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Both are assessed on argument quality, not on content knowledge, and both are where a tutor's boundary matters most. Support means reading the student's own draft and asking the questions a reader would ask. It never means supplying text, and a student who hands in supplied text is exposed to a malpractice finding.

ib-tuition.regionsTitle: Where you live, and whose rules you are working under
ib-tuition.regionsIntro: Online delivery means the emirate you live in changes the paperwork around your child's schooling rather than the availability of a specialist. It is worth knowing which it is, because the authority named on your school's licence is the one whose published guidance applies to you.

regions.name: Dubai
regions.note: Licensed by KHDA, which also publishes the mandatory-subject requirements Dubai private schools implement regardless of their licensed curriculum. The largest IB cluster in the country, and the one gaining three new IB schools in the 2026-27 intake, so also the emirate where transfer-driven tuition requests concentrate.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi
regions.note: Licensed by ADEK, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK also sets professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff, which is why a family here cannot simply pay their child's own class teacher for extra hours after school.

regions.name: Al Ain
regions.note: Also under ADEK, with a smaller set of schools offering the full Diploma. Families here more often face the subject-availability problem rather than the choice problem: the Higher Level combination a student wants may exist at one school in the city, which makes online specialist access the practical answer.

regions.name: Sharjah
regions.note: The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in the emirate and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. A Sharjah family moving to a Dubai school is therefore moving between two different approval regimes, not just two campuses.

regions.name: Ajman
regions.note: The federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools here, as it does in Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Diploma provision is thin, and a number of Ajman families commute into Sharjah or Dubai schools, which pushes any weekday tuition slot late into the evening.

regions.name: Ras Al Khaimah
regions.note: The Department of Knowledge regulates private education in the emirate and, like Sharjah's authority, approves fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods. RAK returns almost no mentions across the competing pages in this market, which tells you how much tutoring attention the emirate gets.

regions.name: Fujairah
regions.note: Under the federal Ministry of Education. The east coast's distance from the IB cluster on the Dubai side of the country is exactly the case where a travelling tutor is not a realistic option and a live online specialist is the only way to reach a Higher Level subject teacher.

regions.name: Umm Al Quwain
regions.note: Also supervised federally by the Ministry of Education. Families here typically hold a school place in a neighbouring emirate, so the school run already consumes the early evening and sessions are scheduled accordingly rather than at the 4pm slot a Dubai family might take.

schoolClusters.note: The deepest IB cluster in the country, running continuum schools alongside schools that offer the Diploma on top of a British Middle Years route. Students we support attend schools across this group; the mix of models is why two Dubai families can describe completely different experiences of the same programme.

schoolClusters.city: Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, licensed by ADEK
schoolClusters.note: A smaller Diploma set spread across the island, Khalifa City and Al Ain, which means Higher Level combinations are more constrained by a single school's timetable than by a student's ability. Families here are the most frequent users of out-of-school specialist teaching for a subject their school offers at one level only.

Thinner provision, three different regulatory regimes across the group, and long commutes that push the realistic start of a weekday session past seven in the evening. This is where online delivery stops being a preference and becomes the only way to reach a subject specialist at all.

ib-tuition.modesIntro: Four ways families use tuition inside a UAE school year, in roughly the order they tend to ask for them. Each is one-to-one and delivered over live video; what changes is the length of the commitment and what the sessions are pointed at.

modes.title: Transition block before a programme starts
modes.description: Six to ten weeks for a student moving from IGCSE, MYP, CBSE or an American high school programme into the Diploma, usually across the summer or the term before the switch. The point is not to pre-teach the course. It is to close the specific gap the new programme assumes, so the first term is spent learning rather than catching up.

modes.description: The standard pattern: one fixed hour a week per subject, same specialist, held through the term so that the work tracks the school's own sequence rather than running parallel to it. The tutor works from the current subject guide and from whatever the school has set, which is why the first thing we ask for is the school and the year group.

modes.title: Coursework clinics on the student's own draft
modes.description: Short, intensive sessions for the Internal Assessment, the Extended Essay and the Theory of Knowledge essay, built around a draft the student has already written. The tutor reads it and asks the questions a reader would ask: what is the research question, does the data answer it, where does the argument assert rather than show. No text is supplied.

modes.description: A short block of concentrated work in the weeks before papers, usually two or three sessions a week in one or two subjects. It is built on past-paper technique and command-term discipline rather than on new content, because at that point in the year content coverage is the school's work and marks are won on execution.

sections.heading: What IB tuition in the UAE has to work around
paragraphs: IB tuition in the UAE is one-to-one teaching in a named IB subject, delivered over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time, with a free trial lesson first. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address anywhere in the country. That is the delivery answer. The more useful answer is about supply, and it starts with a number almost nobody in this market publishes.

Dubai's private sector held 387,441 students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula, split 37% UK curriculum, 26% Indian, 14% American and 7% International Baccalaureate, as reported by the Dubai Media Office in January 2025. An IB family is shopping inside a tutoring market whose depth was built for other boards. A tutor who has taught A-Level Chemistry for a decade knows the chemistry; whether they know how a scientific investigation is marked, or what the moderation of a school's internal marks does to a predicted grade, is a separate question that a parent has to ask explicitly.

The share figures also explain a pattern UAE parents notice and cannot account for: tuition that produces confident homework and no movement in the school grade. Content help lifts classwork. Grades in the Diploma move when a student changes what they do in the assessment itself, which means working from the current subject guide, the command terms and the criteria the school is marking against. That requires a specialist in the programme rather than in the subject alone, and at 7% of the student body, specialists in the programme are not the people who answer a local advertisement.

sections.heading: Which authority licenses your child's school, and what it actually approves
paragraphs: Most writing about UAE education stops at inspection. Inspection is the visible part, but it is not the part that constrains a family. Approval is. The government's own guidance on u.ae sets out the map: ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in Abu Dhabi; KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai; the Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in Sharjah; Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge does the same in that emirate; and the Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

Two of those authorities go further than oversight. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's bodies approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Read that again as a parent: a change to what a school teaches, and how it assesses, is something the emirate signs off. At federal level the baseline is narrower. Private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That single sentence is why a UAE school can run the IB at all, and also why every IB school here carries the Ministry subjects alongside it.

Fees sit in the same frame. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for Dubai private schools for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. For a tuition budget that is useful context rather than trivia: if the school fee is flat for the year, the question of what an extra weekly hour is worth gets a cleaner answer than it would in a year of fee rises. None of this makes any tutoring provider approved by any of these bodies. IB Gram holds no licence, permit or endorsement from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and nothing on this page should be read as implying one.

sections.heading: Moving school, curriculum or emirate part-way through
paragraphs: This is the most common reason a UAE family starts IB tuition, and the one no competing page maps. The country's school population moves. Dubai alone is adding seven new private schools for 2026-27, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six schools opened in 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6%, according to KHDA. Every new place is a transfer from somewhere, and a meaningful share of those transfers happen in the middle of a two-year programme.

A transfer is not a uniform event. Moving from IGCSE into the Diploma is a change of assessment philosophy: from a syllabus you can finish to criteria you have to satisfy, and from past papers as the main currency to internal assessment carrying real weight. Moving from CBSE is a change of pace and of what counts as an answer. Moving within the same programme but across emirates is the gentlest version and still costs a term, because the receiving school's internal sequence, internal deadlines and coursework supervision arrangements are different from the ones your child left.

The practical mistake families make is to treat the move as an administrative task and the academic consequence as something that will even out. It does not even out by itself in a programme this short. A student who joins a Diploma cohort in November has missed the setting of at least one Internal Assessment and the first round of feedback on it. The fix is specific and bounded: identify the two or three real gaps, close them in a transition block, and get a written note of what was covered that the new school's teacher can read. That is a six-to-ten-week job, not a two-year subscription.

sections.heading: Entries, records and the paperwork a mid-year move lands on
paragraphs: Examination entries are made by the school, months before the papers, and that single fact catches more UAE transfer families than any other. Cambridge publishes the pattern clearly for its own series: for the March 2027 series the examination period runs 3 February to 4 March 2027, final entries are due 27 November 2026, forecast grades are due 27 February 2027, results reach centres on Direct on 13 May and certificates follow in late June. Entries close more than two months before the first paper. A family changing school in January is changing school after the window has shut.

Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination because the wrong zone timetable was used. Pearson Edexcel runs International GCSE in May/June and November, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026; June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, while November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live official timetable is always the document to work from rather than any restatement of it, including this one.

For the IB the position is different and worth stating honestly: no IB session or results date on this site has been confirmed against the IB's own publication, because ibo.org blocks automated checking. UAE schools sit the May session. Beyond that, ask your child's IB coordinator for the registration and upload deadlines in writing, and treat anything else you read online as unverified. Those internal upload deadlines are the ones a transfer actually threatens, because they are the dates on which a school has to submit work that a student may have begun under a different supervisor.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural Studies: which class your child is in
paragraphs: These subjects run alongside the IB, not instead of parts of it, and in Dubai the requirements are published in detail. KHDA's mandatory-subject guidance makes Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with the requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For a Diploma student this is timetable time that the six IB subjects do not get, and it appears on the school report.

Placement is not a preference. KHDA requires that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. The language rules follow from that: Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

Two further details shape what outside support can usefully do. KHDA requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach these subjects, which is a school-level credential and not something a private tutor can substitute for. And for these mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. So support here means working with the material the school is using, building the language the subject is taught in, and practising the written forms the assessment asks for. It does not mean importing a parallel syllabus, and any provider offering one has not read the guidance. Instructional time, incidentally, is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes.
