sections.heading: Which authority approves a fee, and which has nothing to say about yours
paragraphs: Sharjah's authority and Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods for the schools they regulate. That is a genuinely broad remit, and it is routinely misread by parents and by provider websites into something it does not cover. Approval of a school's fee is not approval of a tutor's fee. No authority in the UAE approves, publishes or caps what a private tutor charges.

The practical value of knowing your regulator is different. It tells you which inspection report exists and where to read it, which channel answers a question about the school's curriculum or fee, and which rules bind the teachers your child already has. ADEK supervises licensing and accreditation in Abu Dhabi and Al Ain, and its professional-ethics position reported for private and charter school staff is the reason the obvious option, paying your child's own teacher, is the wrong one to pursue in the capital.

It also tells you which claims to disbelieve. A tutoring provider cannot be approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education or an examination board in the way those words are usually deployed on a tutoring website. KHDA does issue an Educational Services Permit, but that is a permit for a training institute with premises, with initial approval first and a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps. IB Gram holds none of these, says so, and teaches over live video instead.

sections.heading: The Ministry hours already inside the fee you pay
paragraphs: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. Those hours are already on your child's timetable and already inside the school fee you pay. Any tutoring budget should start by noticing that.

The rules are specific enough to be checkable. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language; Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students; the school's licensed-curriculum language applies for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. Teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic require appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects.

Two of these details should change how you read an offer. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, and KHDA advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes, so a provider matching a school's lesson length is not matching a tutoring hour. And the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry, is prohibited for these subjects. A provider advertising its own Arabic or Social Studies syllabus for a Dubai school pupil is advertising material the school could not adopt. Supporting the school's own content is legitimate; replacing it is not.

sections.heading: Equivalency: the cheapest thing to get wrong and the dearest to discover late
paragraphs: A Ministry of Education equivalency file is where a UAE family discovers whether two years of subject choices actually add up. The reported British-track rule is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. That exclusion is the detail that catches families who counted them.

For the American track, the reported requirements are English proficiency evidenced by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics evidenced by at least 450 in the SAT Mathematics test. A ranking page in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects. The reported rule is five. Publishing the right count matters more than publishing a confident one.

For the IB Diploma we will not publish a points threshold. The source that set out the British and American requirements states none, and we could not read an IB figure on the Ministry's own pages, so putting one here would be an invention dressed as guidance. Check with the Ministry channel and your school's Diploma coordinator. Nothing in this process requires tutoring, and no provider, including this one, performs or guarantees equivalency. What tutoring can do is make sure the subject count and grades that the file will need are in place while there is still time to influence them.

sections.heading: The dates we will print, and the ones we will not
paragraphs: Every spending decision in an exam year is really a date decision, and the dates belong to the boards rather than to the school or the tutor. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Its March 2027 series is published in full: papers from 3 February to 4 March 2027, final entries due 27 November 2026, forecast grades due 27 February 2027, results on Direct on 13 May and certificates in late June.

Read those two lines together and the planning point is obvious. The entry deadline sits more than two months before the first paper. A decision about whether your child is entered, and for which tier, has to be made while the teaching is still in progress. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, and it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone; Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone timetable was used. Ask your exams officer which zone your centre sits in before you build a revision plan around a Cambridge exam zone timetable.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations run in May or June and in November. The November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, including International GCSE November 2027, and provisional dates can be revised, so always open the live timetable rather than trusting a date restated on a website. For the IB Diploma we publish no session or results dates at all, because we could not read them from the IB itself.

sections.heading: Six checks, and where each one is actually answered
paragraphs: Most of what decides whether a tutoring arrangement was worth the money is settled before the first lesson, in answers a parent can get in one conversation. None of the six checks below needs a specialist to evaluate. Each has a weak answer that sounds reassuring, which is why the fourth column exists. A provider who answers all six plainly is telling you something about how the rest of the arrangement will run.

The permit question is first because it is binary and because the answer identifies the category of person teaching. The own-school question matters most in Abu Dhabi, where the reported ethics position for private and charter school staff bars paid tutoring of pupils enrolled at their own school. The board question is the one families most often cannot answer: Cambridge and Pearson set different papers and different syllabus codes for subjects that share a name, and a tutor who has not asked which one your child sits has not started work.

The last two are about money and data. Settle in writing what the fee covers per 60 minutes, what sits outside it, the notice period for moving a session, and who absorbs a late cancellation. Then ask what personal information about your child is collected, why, and how to have it deleted; UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on personal data protection is the reason that question is reasonable, and a form that asks for a minor's school, grades and photograph without stating a purpose is the reason it is necessary.

sections.heading: Why a UAE family buys this online, and what that changes in the price
paragraphs: Searches for an IB home tutor are among the most common in this market, and the honest answer has two halves. The first half is what the market charges for a visiting arrangement: published UAE figures run from AED 180 to 350 on Bestimate's 2026 table and from AED 200 to 500 in home-tutor listings, with monthly packages of AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour visits. Travel is inside those numbers whether or not it appears on the invoice.

The second half is what the travel costs in something other than dirhams. A tutor who must reach your address is a tutor drawn from a radius, not from the country, and the radius is what prices your subject. A family in Fujairah or Umm Al Quwain searching inside a 30-minute drive is searching a pool that may contain nobody who has taught Chemistry at Higher Level. A family in Dubai searching the same way during the evening peak is paying for time spent on Sheikh Zayed Road. That is the mechanism, and it is why the published in-home bands sit above the online ones for the same qualification.

IB Gram delivers one-to-one IB tuition over live video everywhere in the Emirates. Home visits are part of our service in India and not in the UAE, and no arrangement here involves anyone arriving at a UAE address. What the format buys is selection: the family in Fujairah and the family in Emirates Hills choose from the same group of subject specialists, in an evening slot fixed in Gulf Standard Time, with the lesson recorded in the student's own notes rather than in a drive. Online IB tutoring in Dubai and in the northern emirates is the same product, which is not true of the alternative.

sections.heading: Academic honesty is a budget line, not a footnote
paragraphs: There is one purchase in this market that is worth nothing at any price, and it is sold openly. A page in this SERP offers a finished Internal Assessment for AED 3,750. A student who submits assessed work that is not their own is exposed to an IB malpractice finding, and a malpractice finding can cost the Diploma. No hourly saving elsewhere compensates for that, and no provider's reassurance changes what the IB does about it.

The boundary is not vague and it is not restrictive in a way that hurts teaching. A tutor may teach the assessment criteria and what each one asks for, work through examples that are not the student's task, help a student plan and narrow a research question, read a draft the student has written and say where it falls short of a criterion, teach the referencing convention, and rehearse the oral components. The student does the writing, the data collection, the analysis and the revision, every time.

What a tutor may not do is supply text, rewrite a passage into its final form, or hand over work for submission. There is a second line worth knowing about: IB, Cambridge and Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables are not ours to distribute, so we reference and link them rather than sending copies. A provider who offers a library of mark schemes as an inclusion in the fee is offering something they should not, and billing you for it.

process.title: Tell us the component, not just the subject
process.description: Send the board, the syllabus code where you have it, the level, and which part of the course is the problem. "Chemistry HL, Cambridge-style practical work, internal assessment due in six weeks" gets a useful match. "Science help" does not. The more precisely the need is described, the smaller the gap between the first tutor suggested and the right one.

process.title: We check the calendar before the diary
process.description: Your child's board and series decide which weeks matter. We look at the published entry deadline and exam window for that series, and the school's own internal deadlines for assessed components, before proposing a start date. A plan built on the calendar month rather than the board's dates usually buys hours in the wrong weeks.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with its conditions stated
process.description: One lesson at no charge, with the tutor who would teach the course, so the match is judged on teaching rather than on a profile. No payment is taken beforehand and there is no obligation to continue. If the fit is wrong, say so and we will propose a different tutor or tell you we do not have one.

process.title: Agree the fee and the terms in writing
process.description: Before the first paid session you get the fee per 60 minutes of teaching, what sits outside it, the notice period for moving a lesson, and what personal information we hold about your child and why. Market bands on this page are other providers' published figures; your own figure is confirmed in writing to you.

process.title: A fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time
process.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video, in a slot held for the term and set in UAE time rather than the tutor's. Post-iftar timing during Ramadan is a scheduling change, not a renegotiation. If a session has to move, the notice period you agreed applies to both sides.

process.title: Review each term against the component
process.description: Progress is read against the thing being assessed: the paper, the criterion, the component weighting. Each term we say what has moved, what has not, and whether the hours should continue, change shape or stop. A recommendation to stop is a real outcome and we will give it when it is the right one.

whyPoints.title: Every figure carries its source and its date
whyPoints.description: The AED bands on this page name the provider or rate tracker that published them and the month they were read. No figure is presented as ours, and no number appears without somewhere to check it. Three of the most visible pages in this market publish no price at all, and two more quote in US dollars.

whyPoints.title: We say what we are not
whyPoints.description: IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and no UAE office or centre. Naming a regulator and explaining what it does is useful to you. Implying it endorses us would not be.

whyPoints.title: The honesty line is written down
whyPoints.description: What a tutor may teach, read and give feedback on, and what has to be the student's own work, is set out on the page rather than left to be negotiated under deadline pressure. That boundary protects the Diploma, which is the only thing the whole arrangement exists to defend.

whyPoints.title: Dates come from the boards, or not at all
whyPoints.description: Cambridge and Pearson dates here are taken from those boards' own published timetables and key-date documents. For the IB we publish no session or results date, because we could not verify one from the IB itself. A wrong date in a planning table is worse than a blank one.

whyPoints.title: Selection rather than proximity
whyPoints.description: Teaching over live video means the choice of tutor is made on who has taught the component, not on who can reach your area by 5pm. For Higher Level subjects in the northern emirates, that difference is the whole of the available choice rather than a preference.

whyPoints.title: An honest answer when we cannot help
whyPoints.description: Some components have very few experienced teachers anywhere, and sometimes the hour you need is already taken. We will tell you that, rather than fill the slot with somebody who has not taught it. Being told no in October is cheaper than finding out in March.

faqs.question: Who actually sets the price of an IB tutor in the UAE, and is any of it regulated?
faqs.answer: The provider sets it. No UAE authority approves, publishes or caps what a private tutor may charge. KHDA, ADEK, SPEA and the Department of Knowledge approve school tuition fees and curricula for the schools they regulate, and in Sharjah and Ras Al Khaimah that extends to courses and assessment methods, but none of them touches a private lesson fee. What regulation does is shape supply: the curriculum your school is licensed for, the subjects the Ministry requires alongside it, and who may lawfully be paid to teach privately. Published UAE market rates ran from AED 33 to AED 650 an hour in October 2026, which is what an unregulated market looks like.

faqs.question: The private tuition permit is issued free, so what is in a rate of AED 300 an hour?
faqs.answer: Not licensing. The MoHRE private tuition work permit is granted free of charge for two years and issued in about two working days, so it costs a tutor nothing to be lawful. What sits inside a higher rate is scarcity of a specific kind: someone who has taught your child's exact component at that level, repeatedly, and has marked work against its criteria. That describes very few people in a country where the IB accounts for roughly 7 per cent of Dubai's private-school enrolment. Ask what the person has taught and for how many cohorts. If the answer is about certificates rather than components, the premium is buying the wrong thing.

faqs.question: Dubai capped private school fees for 2026-27. Should tutoring prices have moved too?
faqs.answer: They are unrelated mechanisms. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not increase for 2026-27, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion. That decision binds schools, which need fee approval. Tutoring has no approval step and no cap, so nothing obliges a provider to hold its rate. In the same period Dubai licensed seven new private schools adding 16,846 places, three of them IB, and new schools recruit experienced IB teachers from the same pool families hire from in the evenings. The fixed line in your budget this year is the school fee, not the tutoring.

faqs.question: Does KHDA or ADEK approve tutoring providers, and should I only use one that is?
faqs.answer: No tutoring provider can hold the approval that phrase implies. KHDA issues an Educational Services Permit to training institutes with premises in Dubai, which involves initial approval, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal. That permit is about a business and its building, not about any tutor inside it. ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools. Neither body certifies individual tutors or online providers. A website claiming regulator approval for tutoring is describing something that does not exist, which is a reason to read the rest of its claims carefully.

faqs.question: If we move from Dubai to Abu Dhabi mid-Diploma, which authority's rules follow us?
faqs.answer: The authority follows the school, not the family. A Dubai school sits under KHDA; an Abu Dhabi or Al Ain school sits under ADEK, which supervises licensing and accreditation in the emirate. What changes on a move is which inspection report exists, which channel answers questions about fees and curriculum, and which professional-ethics rules bind your child's teachers. The Diploma itself does not change, and nor do the board deadlines. For tutoring, nothing changes at all: the fee was never approved by either authority, and lessons over live video continue unchanged across an emirate border or an international one.

faqs.question: Is an IB hour genuinely scarcer than an IGCSE hour in the UAE, or is that just marketing?
faqs.answer: It is arithmetic. Dubai's private schools held 387,441 students in 2024-25, with UK-curriculum schools at 37 per cent of enrolment and the IB at 7 per cent. Before you narrow by subject, the pool of adults who have taught the Diploma is far smaller than the pool who have taught IGCSE. Narrow it to Higher Level, then to a specific component such as Paper 3 or exploration supervision, and the remaining number is small. That is why published specialist bands sit at AED 200 to 450 and above while a qualified online IGCSE subject tutor starts around AED 150. The gap tracks supply, not difficulty.

faqs.question: Should we pay for Arabic or Islamic Education when the school has to teach them anyway?
faqs.answer: Start from what is already included. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, and those hours are inside the school fee you already pay. Outside support is reasonable for practice, feedback and the school's own assessment tasks. It is not reasonable as a parallel syllabus: the use of different or additional content for these subjects without prior Ministry permission is prohibited. Also note that teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education in schools need appropriate KHDA approval, which is a useful question to ask of anyone offering to teach them privately.

faqs.question: Why is my child in a different Arabic class from their friend at the same school?
faqs.answer: Because KHDA requires it. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited, because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Arabic as a first language and for Islamic Education for Arab students, while non-Arab students take Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with KHDA advising at least 25 minutes for any mandatory-subject lesson.

faqs.question: What subject count does an equivalency file actually need from an IGCSE student?
faqs.answer: Five. The reported British-track requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. At least one ranking page in this market states six, which is a count worth checking before it shapes a subject choice. Verify the current requirement on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate attestation channel, because the consequence of a shortfall only appears at the end of two years.

faqs.question: Is there an IB points figure for UAE equivalency we can plan around?
faqs.answer: Not one we will publish. The July 2026 reporting that set out the British and American track requirements states no IB points threshold, and we could not read one on the Ministry's own pages, so any number here would be invention. The American-track requirements that are reported are English evidenced by IELTS academic 5, TOEFL iBT 61 or SAT reading and writing 450, and mathematics evidenced by SAT Mathematics of at least 450. For the IB, ask the Ministry channel and your school's Diploma coordinator. Equivalency is a process we describe, not one IB Gram performs, arranges or guarantees for anyone.

faqs.question: Why will you not print the IB exam dates on a page about cost?
faqs.answer: Because we could not verify them. The IB's own site returns an error to automated checking, so no IB session or results date in this project was confirmed from the IB itself, and a wrong date in a planning table is worse than no date. Cambridge and Pearson publish theirs and we use them: Cambridge's March 2027 series runs 3 February to 4 March 2027 with final entries due 27 November 2026, and Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE timetable runs to 19 November 2026. For the Diploma, take the session dates from your school's coordinator or from ibo.org and build the spending plan on those.

faqs.question: What does the Cambridge zone system change about when we should buy hours?
faqs.answer: It changes which timetable your plan is built on. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, and it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone; Cambridge states it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after the wrong zone version was used. Two children in the same UAE city can sit the same paper on different days if their centres sit in different zones. Ask your exams officer for the zone before scheduling a revision block, because a block timed to the wrong version wastes the most expensive weeks in the year.

faqs.question: A teacher from my child's own school has offered paid evening lessons. Should we take it?
faqs.answer: Treat it with care, and check the school's position first. Reporting on Abu Dhabi indicates that ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. The conflict is obvious once stated: the same person would be teaching, assessing and privately charging for the same course. Verify the current rule with the school and the authority rather than relying on the arrangement being common.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a tutor's permit and a tuition centre's licence?
faqs.answer: They cover different objects. An individual's private tuition work permit comes from MoHRE under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is free for two years, and says the person may lawfully be paid for lessons. A tuition business with premises and staff in Dubai needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least 30 days before expiry. A centre holding the second does not tell you anything about the individual teaching your child's hour, which is the thing to ask about.

faqs.question: How are lessons actually delivered to a family in the Emirates?
faqs.answer: One-to-one over live video, in a slot fixed in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send anyone to a UAE address; home visits are part of what we offer in India only. The published UAE market shows why the online format is the better buy here: travel-inclusive bands run from AED 180 to 500 an hour against online bands from AED 150 to 300 for comparable qualifications, and a visiting tutor is drawn from a driving radius rather than from the whole subject pool. A family in Fujairah and a family in Dubai choose from the same specialists on the same terms.

faqs.question: What happens to the cost if nobody is free for our subject and our hour?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and nothing is charged. Some components have very few experienced teachers in any market, and evening slots in the weeks before a published series are the ones everybody wants. In that case the options are a different hour, a short block aimed only at the component rather than a weekly slot, or a wait with a date attached. What we will not do is fill the slot with somebody who has not taught the component and let you discover it in the third lesson. An honest no in October costs less than the wrong yes in March.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with an Internal Assessment without crossing the IB's honesty rules?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor can teach what each criterion asks for, work through examples that are not your child's task, help narrow a research question, read a draft your child has written and say where it falls short, teach the referencing convention and rehearse an oral. Your child does the writing, the data work, the analysis and the revision. Anything presented as finished work for submission is malpractice, and a page in this market openly sells a completed Internal Assessment for AED 3,750. The saving is irrelevant next to a malpractice finding, which can cost the whole Diploma.

ib-tutor-cost.closingHeading: Price the hour against the rules, then book the week that matters
ib-tutor-cost.closingBody: An IB tutor cost in the UAE only means something once you know which component it buys, which board's deadline it is racing, and what the school is already required to deliver. The market bands on this page are other providers' published figures, dated and attributed, so you can hold any quote up against them. What we offer is one-to-one IB tuition over live video across all seven emirates, a free trial lesson with its conditions stated, and the fee per 60 minutes in writing before anything is paid. Send the board, the level and the component, and we will tell you what is realistic or that we cannot help.

ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Arabic A Language and Literature, Arabic A Literature, Arabic B and ab initio, and support Arabic first-language students in English-medium Diploma subjects. Several teach in both languages, which matters most in the sciences.

intro.heading: Two systems apply to the same child, and both of them are enforceable
paragraphs: Arabic-speaking families in the UAE sit at an intersection no other group occupies. Their child may be taking Arabic as a first language inside the IB, which is an academically demanding literature course, while simultaneously taking Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies as subjects the emirate regulator requires of every private school regardless of its licensed curriculum. These are not the same obligation, they are not assessed the same way, and conflating them is the commonest reason a strong Arabic speaker ends up with a disappointing Arabic grade.

The regulator side is specific. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school teaches, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction.

The language of instruction is prescribed too. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language. Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils. For non-Arabs, Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies are delivered in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes.

The IB side is a different problem. Arabic A Language and Literature and Arabic A Literature are full studies-in-language-and-literature courses, marked on close reading, comparative argument and oral analysis, in formal Standard Arabic. A student who speaks Levantine, Gulf or Egyptian Arabic at home and reads comfortably is not automatically equipped for that, because the course assesses literary analysis in a formal register rather than fluency. Conversely a student with strong spoken Arabic placed in Arabic B is capped at a level below what they could achieve.

Placement, then, is the decision that matters most, and it is made by the school in the first weeks. An IB tutor for arabic speaking students in the UAE earns their fee largely by getting that decision examined before it hardens: reading the student's writing in Standard Arabic, comparing it with what the course demands, and giving the family something concrete to take to the coordinator. After that the teaching is ordinary subject teaching, and it is finite.

Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not provide in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; those are offered only in India. For Arabic first-language teaching the online format matters more than usual, because a specialist in Arabic A Literature is a narrow speciality and families in Sharjah, Ajman, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah will rarely find one within driving distance.

ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.programmesIntro: Arabic runs through every IB programme in the UAE, but what is assessed changes at each stage, and so does the regulator's requirement sitting alongside it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external examinations, transdisciplinary units rather than subject periods, and Arabic taught as a language within the programme while also meeting the regulator's mandatory requirement. The usual issue at this stage is reading fluency in Standard Arabic, which diverges early from the dialect spoken at home and rarely gets separate attention.
programmes.countryNote: This is where the Arab and non-Arab streams first separate under KHDA's rules, and where a placement decision quietly sets a child's path for a decade. A first-language stream assumes home support with reading; a family that speaks Arabic but reads mainly in English should say so rather than assume the school has inferred it.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Language and literature in Arabic is assessed against criteria covering analysis, organisation, language use and producing text, each on a one-to-eight scale. Students who speak Arabic confidently and write it rarely lose marks on the producing-text criterion, which is about register and structure rather than about vocabulary.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP years are when the gap between spoken and written Arabic becomes visible in grades, and when it is cheapest to fix. A student who reaches DP1 reading Standard Arabic slowly will struggle with Arabic A Literature regardless of how fluently they speak, and three years of MYP is ample time to close that if anyone names it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Arabic can appear as a studies-in-language-and-literature subject at Higher or Standard Level, or as a language acquisition subject in Arabic B or ab initio. A student can also work towards the Bilingual Diploma by taking two languages at the studies-in-language-and-literature level, which is a real distinction on a university application and a heavy workload.
programmes.countryNote: In the UAE the Diploma sits alongside the mandatory subjects, so an Arabic first-language student may be studying Arabic A for the IB and Islamic Education in Standard Arabic as a regulator requirement, with Social Studies also delivered in Arabic. That is a substantial Arabic-medium load inside an otherwise English-medium timetable, and it is worth mapping before Higher Levels are chosen.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE Arabic
programmes.description: Many UAE schools run IGCSE before the Diploma, with Cambridge offering Arabic as a First Language under syllabus code 0508 and Arabic as a Foreign Language under 0544. The two are entirely different examinations, and the entry decision has the same shape as the Arabic A or B decision two years later.
programmes.countryNote: The IGCSE Arabic entry is where a misplacement first becomes visible on a certificate rather than in a report. It also interacts with equivalency: Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five accredited subjects the Ministry of Education requires on the British track, so a family relying on Arabic to make up the five would be caught out.

ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.subjectsIntro: Two groups of subjects matter to Arabic-speaking families: the Arabic courses themselves, and the English-medium subjects where an Arabic first-language student carries a specific, fixable disadvantage.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Literary and non-literary texts analysed in formal Standard Arabic, with a guided analysis paper, a comparative essay paper and an individual oral. Fluent speakers lose marks on structure and register rather than on comprehension, and the comparative paper is where most of the difference between a 5 and a 7 sits.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Literature
subjects.description: Narrower and deeper than Language and Literature: literary works only, with close reading and comparative analysis across texts and periods. The demand is reading stamina in Standard Arabic and a critical vocabulary, both of which have to be built deliberately rather than assumed from being a native speaker.

subjects.name: Arabic B
subjects.description: A language acquisition course assessing listening, reading, writing and speaking in defined text types. The right course for a non-Arab student with several years of Arabic, and the wrong one for a near-native speaker, because the assessment ceiling does not reward the extra ability. Placement is the whole question here.

subjects.name: Arabic ab initio
subjects.description: For genuine beginners, available at Standard Level only, with a grade ceiling that reflects the level of the course. Non-Arab students in the mandatory Arabic stream sometimes have more Arabic than ab initio assumes, which is an argument for checking the placement rather than accepting the default.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.levels: School-mandated stream, not an IB subject
subjects.description: A regulator requirement rather than an IB course, taught in Standard Arabic for Arab pupils and in the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs. KHDA requires separate classes by group and prohibits different or additional content without prior Ministry permission, which means support has to mean teaching the approved material well.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies and Moral, Social and Cultural studies
subjects.levels: School-mandated stream, not an IB subject
subjects.description: Social Studies is delivered with Arabic as the primary language for Arab pupils, while non-Arab pupils take Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language. Both sit in the weekly timetable alongside the IB programme and reduce the periods available to everything else.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The component that most often limits an Arabic first-language student's total is the unseen analysis paper, where time pressure and idiom combine. The fix is reading speed and a repertoire of analytical sentence structures, which are trainable, rather than general English practice.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: The correct course for a student whose schooling before the UAE was Arabic-medium, and a placement worth questioning if the student has been in English-medium education for years. Productive writing in specified text types, marked on register and audience, is the part that responds fastest to teaching.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Mathematical ability transfers across languages; the wording of problems does not. Students educated partly in Arabic often lose marks on multi-clause worded questions rather than on technique, and practising the reading of questions is a distinct exercise from practising the mathematics.

subjects.name: Physics and Chemistry
subjects.description: Technical vocabulary is the specific barrier. A student who understands a concept in Arabic and meets it in English for the first time in DP1 has a translation problem that reads as a knowledge gap. Bilingual tutors resolve it quickly by teaching the terminology as terminology rather than reteaching the physics.

subjects.name: Business Management and Economics
subjects.description: Both reward applying a named tool to a specific organisation or article in precise English. Arabic first-language students often have the analysis and write it in a register that costs marks. Early sessions are about sentence structure and the expected shape of a commentary rather than about content.

ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.regionsTitle: Arabic requirements are federal; the regulator reading them is not
ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.regionsIntro: The mandatory-subject obligation has a federal basis, but each emirate's authority applies and inspects it, which changes what a family can ask for and whom they ask.

regions.name: Dubai
regions.note: KHDA publishes the mandatory-subject guidelines that set lesson units, separate classes by group and languages of instruction, and requires that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects. That is a checkable credential a parent can reasonably ask the school about.

regions.name: Abu Dhabi and Al Ain
regions.note: ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate and applies its own framework rather than the KHDA bands. ADEK is named by almost no tutoring provider online, so Arabic-speaking families in the capital are routinely reading guidance written for Dubai schools.

regions.name: Sharjah
regions.note: The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. Because curriculum approval sits with the regulator, a request for an Arabic course the school does not currently run is a regulatory question as well as a timetabling one.

regions.name: Ras Al Khaimah
regions.note: The Department of Knowledge regulates private education and likewise approves fees, curricula, programmes and assessment methods. A small market, which in practice means Arabic A Literature at Higher Level may not be timetabled at all, and online delivery is the only route to a specialist.

regions.name: Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah
regions.note: The federal Ministry of Education supervises private schools in these three emirates. The federal baseline is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations.

regions.name: Across the Gulf
regions.note: Families who move between the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait and Oman during a Diploma face a different Arabic curriculum requirement in each jurisdiction while the IB course stays constant. Online delivery keeps the IB side continuous across a relocation, which is the part that cannot be restarted.

regions.name: Returning from abroad
regions.note: Students who spent primary school in Europe or North America often speak Arabic at home and read it slowly, and are placed in an Arabic first-language stream on the basis of the home language alone. That mismatch is the single most common Arabic placement error, and it is detectable in one piece of written work.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools with substantial Arabic first-language cohorts
schoolClusters.note: Schools whose students IB Gram tutors support. They appear as context about where Arabic first-language and bilingual provision sits in the market, not as any relationship. Arabic streams and course offerings differ by year group, so confirm what is timetabled with the school itself.

schoolClusters.note: Outside Dubai the regulator differs and so does the published guidance. Arabic A Literature at Higher Level is a narrow speciality in these markets, and option blocks are correspondingly tighter, which is the practical reason online specialist support is used here more than in Dubai.

modes.description: A short piece of work that establishes which Arabic course actually fits: the student writes a piece in Standard Arabic and reads an unseen literary extract, and a first-language specialist reports on whether Arabic A, Arabic B or ab initio is the right level. The output is something a family can take to the IB coordinator.

modes.description: One or two sessions a week on the components that carry the marks: guided textual analysis, the comparative essay, and the individual oral. Work is in Standard Arabic throughout, against the published assessment criteria for the student's own course and level.

sections.heading: Which Arabic course your child is actually sitting
paragraphs: Families often describe the situation as my child takes Arabic, which inside the IB covers at least four distinct courses with different content, different assessment and different grade ceilings. Arabic A Language and Literature studies literary and non-literary texts. Arabic A Literature studies literary works only. Arabic B is a language acquisition course for students with several years of the language. Arabic ab initio is for beginners and exists at Standard Level alone. The distance between the top of ab initio and the top of Arabic A Higher Level is enormous.

Being a native speaker does not settle the question, because the courses are not measuring fluency. Arabic A is measuring literary analysis in formal Standard Arabic: the ability to read an unfamiliar extract closely, argue a reading of it, compare it with another work and sustain that in writing and speech. A student who speaks Gulf or Levantine Arabic at home, watches content in dialect and reads mainly in English can be entirely fluent in conversation and genuinely underprepared for that paper.

The reverse error is just as costly. A non-Arab student who has been in the mandatory Arabic stream of a Dubai school since FS1 may have more Arabic than Arabic B assumes, and considerably more than ab initio. Placing them low protects the school's results and caps the student. It also wastes two years of a Diploma slot that could have carried a stronger grade.

The practical test is not a conversation. It is a piece of written Standard Arabic and an unseen extract, assessed against the descriptors of the course in question. That takes one session, and it produces something concrete to discuss with the IB coordinator rather than an impression. Where the current placement is right, the right answer is to say so and stop.

sections.heading: What the regulator requires alongside the IB programme
paragraphs: The mandatory subjects are not a formality bolted onto an international curriculum, and the published guidelines are unusually precise about how they must run. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 applying to schools whose year starts in April.

Grouping is prescribed. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Language of instruction is prescribed as well: Standard Arabic for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

Time is prescribed by unit rather than by minutes. Mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that the length of any mandatory subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. Content is prescribed too: for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited.

That last rule shapes what any tutoring in these subjects can honestly be. It cannot mean supplying an alternative syllabus or a parallel set of materials. It can mean teaching the approved content well, building reading fluency in Standard Arabic, and preparing a student for the school's own assessments. Schools are also required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a credential question a parent is entitled to ask the school directly.

sections.heading: Arabic A assessment: where the marks sit and where they go missing
paragraphs: A studies-in-language-and-literature course is assessed through a small number of heavily weighted components, which is why a weakness in one of them moves the final grade so much. The guided textual analysis paper puts an unseen extract in front of the student with a question to guide a close reading. The comparative essay paper asks for an argued comparison across studied works. The individual oral requires a global issue examined through two texts. At Higher Level a further written essay is added, and the weightings shift accordingly.

Confirm the exact component weightings for your child's course and year against the current subject guide through the school, because they differ between Language and Literature and Literature and between the two levels. What does not change is the shape of the demand: every component is an argument about a text, written or spoken in formal Standard Arabic, within a fixed time.

Marks go missing in four predictable places. First, paraphrase. A student who retells the extract accurately and does not analyse how meaning is constructed sits in the middle bands however well written the answer. Second, register. Dialect features and informal constructions cost marks in a paper assessed on language use. Third, the comparison itself: two separate essays stapled together score far below a genuinely comparative argument with a line running through it. Fourth, the oral, where students who have not rehearsed under time produce an unstructured ten minutes.

All four respond to practice rather than to content coverage, which is why Arabic A support looks different from science support. Sessions consist of reading unseen extracts cold, writing to time, and having the work scored against the actual criteria. A student who has done that twenty times is a different candidate from one who has read the set texts twenty times.

sections.heading: The Bilingual Diploma, and whether it is worth planning for
paragraphs: A student who takes two languages at the studies-in-language-and-literature level, rather than one plus a language acquisition subject, can qualify for the Bilingual Diploma. For an Arabic first-language student in an English-medium UAE school, Arabic A plus English A is the natural route, and it is a genuine distinction on a university application in a region where bilingual professional competence is valued directly.

It is also a workload decision rather than a prestige one. Two language-and-literature courses means two sets of studied works, two unseen analysis papers and two individual orals, all with reading loads that run across the whole two years. A student carrying that alongside three Higher Level subjects, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge has a genuinely full week, and the mandatory subject periods take more out of the timetable than families expect.

The question to ask is what the distinction buys for the specific destinations on the list. For universities in the Gulf, and for students likely to work professionally in both languages, it can matter. For a student applying to a quantitative degree abroad where the offer is expressed in Higher Level subject grades, the additional language course may cost more in points than the designation is worth. There is no general answer, which is why the decision should be made against a destination list rather than on principle.

Where a family decides to go ahead, the planning point is sequencing. The reading load is front-loadable: set texts can be read in the summer before DP1 and over the first long break, which removes most of the pressure from the second year. Students who leave both sets of texts to be read during term find that the language courses crowd out the subjects carrying the points.

sections.heading: The non-Arab student in a mandatory Arabic stream
paragraphs: A large group of families reading this page are not Arabic-speaking at all: they are families whose child has been in the mandatory Arabic-as-an-additional-language stream since primary school and whose Arabic report has quietly been poor for years. The mandatory subject has no external examination attached in most years, so nothing forces the issue, and then the student reaches an IGCSE or Diploma language decision with several years of Arabic and no measurable attainment.

Two things are worth knowing. The first is that the stream is prescribed: KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, with the licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies, so a non-Arab pupil is not being held back by placement in the additional-language stream. The second is that progress in that stream varies enormously between schools, and a child who has learned very little is not unusual.

The decision point comes at the language acquisition choice. A student with genuine attainment from the mandatory stream may be well placed in Arabic B. A student with years of attendance and little retention is better served by ab initio, or by a different language entirely where the school timetables one. Choosing Arabic B on the basis of years attended rather than attainment is a two-year commitment to a course the student cannot access.

There is one more consideration for families planning university routes through the Ministry of Education's equivalency process. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five accredited subjects required on the British track, so Arabic cannot be used to make up the count. A family relying on it to do so would discover the problem at the point of application.

sections.heading: Ramadan, the UAE calendar and when revision actually happens
paragraphs: The UAE academic year has features no general revision plan accounts for, and Ramadan is the largest. School hours shorten, energy patterns change, and the most productive study window shifts into the evening after iftar. A revision plan built on the assumption of a steady 5pm to 7pm slot five days a week will survive about a fortnight. One built around the actual month works.

The practical adjustments are straightforward once they are planned rather than improvised. Sessions move later, often well after iftar, and families with younger children frequently want them earlier instead. Session length sometimes drops while frequency rises, because concentration in a shorter block is better than endurance in a long one. And the week before Ramadan is worth treating as a deadline for any coursework that would otherwise sit unfinished through it.

The second calendar feature is the sequence of school holidays and the long summer, which falls between the two Diploma years. For Arabic A students specifically, that summer is the single most valuable block of time available, because set texts can be read then rather than during term. Students who arrive in DP2 having read everything have a different year from those who have not.

The third is exam entry, which runs on the boards' calendars rather than on the school year. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries on 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, with forecast grades due 27 February 2027 and results on Direct on 13 May. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November series, with the November 2026 final timetable running to 19 November 2026. For the IB, UAE schools sit the May session, but every date should be confirmed with the school's coordinator or on ibo.org rather than taken from a third-party page, including this one.

sections.heading: Equivalency, attestation and the subjects that do not count
paragraphs: Arabic-speaking families planning UAE university routes meet the Ministry of Education's equivalency process for secondary certificates, and the detail that matters most to them is an exclusion. On the British track, students must submit proof of five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, together with either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

That exclusion changes subject planning in Year 9. A student counting Arabic and Islamic Education towards a total of five will be two subjects short, and the shortfall appears at the point of application rather than at the point of choice. One ranking competitor site in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which is wrong; publishing the correct five-subject rule with its source is a straightforward way to be more accurate than a page that outranks it.

On the American track the requirements are different again: English proficiency is met by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the IB specifically, no points threshold is published on this page, because none could be verified from the Ministry's own material. Ask the Ministry or the emirate attestation authority directly and get the answer in writing.

Two cautions belong with all of this. No tutoring provider performs or guarantees equivalency; it is a process between the family and the authority, and a provider implying otherwise is misdescribing what they sell. And tutoring is not required for equivalency, for university admission or for school progression. Any page suggesting it is has turned a regulatory process into a sales argument.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do with Arabic coursework, and what nobody should
paragraphs: The academic-honesty line is identical in Arabic to every other subject, and it is worth stating in the language of the components. The individual oral must be the student's own spoken analysis. The Higher Level essay must be the student's own writing. An Extended Essay in Arabic A must be the student's own research and argument. A breach of IB academic-honesty rules puts the student's diploma at risk, which is why no provider's convenience is worth it.

What a tutor can do is teach and review. Teach the critical vocabulary and the analytical structures a literary argument needs in Standard Arabic. Explain how each published criterion is applied and show the student what each band looks like in practice. Test whether a chosen global issue is arguable across the two extracts before the oral is prepared. Read a draft the student has written and say where it does not yet meet the criteria. Rehearse the oral under time and review the recording.

What a tutor cannot do is supply text for submission, rework a draft into a finished piece, or provide a prepared oral script. There is a particular temptation in literature subjects, because a fluent adult can produce in twenty minutes what takes a student a week. Any provider offering that is selling the student's diploma, not a service. One operator in this market sells completed internal assessments outright, which is the practice this boundary exists to rule out.

The materials rule applies as well. Published syllabuses, subject guides, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables belong to the IB, Cambridge and Pearson, so the correct practice is to reference and link the official source rather than redistribute copies. And on the tutor's own position: private tutoring in the UAE requires the MoHRE private tutor work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, with those tutoring without one subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted at a family.

process.title: Say which Arabic course the school has placed your child in
process.description: The first useful piece of information is the exact course and level, not the subject name: Arabic A Language and Literature at Higher Level is a different conversation from Arabic B at Standard Level. Add the last report and, if you have it, a piece of the student's written Arabic.

process.title: A free trial lesson with a first-language specialist
process.description: One lesson at no cost, taught in Standard Arabic, used as a working session. The tutor puts an unseen extract in front of the student and reports afterwards on reading stamina, register and analytical vocabulary. If the fit is wrong, a different tutor is proposed before any payment.

process.title: A written view on placement, if placement is the issue
process.description: Where the trial suggests the course level is wrong, you receive a short written assessment against the course descriptors that can be taken to the IB coordinator. Where the placement is right, that is said plainly and the work moves on to the components instead.

process.title: Weekly sessions on the components that carry the marks
process.description: Unseen analysis under time, comparative essay structure, and oral rehearsal, scored against the published criteria for the student's own course. Sessions run in Gulf Standard Time, move later during Ramadan by arrangement, and end with notes naming what was covered and set.

process.title: Reassess at the end of the term
process.description: At term's end the tutor says whether the component weakness has closed. Where it has, support drops to a session before each assessment or stops. Where a different specialism is needed, for instance a bilingual science tutor rather than an Arabic specialist, that is said rather than absorbed.

whyPoints.title: Placement examined before hours are sold
whyPoints.description: The most valuable thing an Arabic specialist can tell some families is that the course level is wrong, which is a conversation with the school rather than a tutoring contract. A placement review is deliberately short and sometimes ends with a recommendation to change nothing.

whyPoints.title: The regulator's rules quoted, not paraphrased
whyPoints.description: Every statement about mandatory subjects on this page comes from the published KHDA guidelines, including the separate-class requirement, the prescribed languages of instruction, the 40-minute lesson unit and the prohibition on unapproved content. IB Gram holds no approval or accreditation from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA or the Ministry of Education, and says so.

whyPoints.title: First-language teaching, not conversational practice
whyPoints.description: Arabic A is a literature course assessed in formal Standard Arabic. The tutors who teach it work on unseen analysis, comparative argument and register, which is a different activity from language practice and the reason a fluent student can still be underprepared.

whyPoints.title: Bilingual support in the English-medium subjects
whyPoints.description: For students whose earlier schooling was Arabic-medium, the barrier in physics or economics is frequently terminology rather than concept. A tutor who can explain in Arabic and then build the English vocabulary around it removes that lag faster than reteaching the subject in English.

whyPoints.title: Online delivery reaches a narrow speciality
whyPoints.description: An Arabic A Literature specialist at Higher Level is not a role a family in Ras Al Khaimah or Fujairah will fill locally. Lessons run live online in Gulf Standard Time, which is what makes the specialist reachable. Home visits are offered only in India, and that is stated rather than implied.

faqs.question: My son speaks Arabic fluently at home. Why is he getting a 4 in Arabic A?
faqs.answer: Because Arabic A is not measuring fluency. It is measuring literary analysis in formal Standard Arabic: reading an unfamiliar extract closely, arguing a reading of it, comparing studied works and sustaining that in writing and speech. A student who speaks Gulf or Levantine Arabic at home, consumes media in dialect and reads mainly in English can be entirely fluent in conversation and genuinely underprepared for the paper. The usual causes are paraphrase instead of analysis, and dialect features in written register. Both respond to timed practice on unseen extracts rather than to more reading of the set texts.

faqs.question: Can we ask the school to move our daughter from Arabic B to Arabic A?
faqs.answer: You can raise it, and the conversation goes better with evidence than with an assertion. The useful preparation is a piece of formal written Standard Arabic and a cold reading of an unseen literary extract, assessed against the Arabic A course descriptors by a first-language specialist. That gives the IB coordinator something to work from. Be prepared for a timetabling answer as well as an academic one: the course has to run in your daughter's cohort and fit her option block. Where the assessment shows the current placement is right, that is worth knowing before the conversation rather than after.

faqs.question: Why does my child have Islamic Education in Arabic when the school teaches the IB in English?
faqs.answer: Because the licensed curriculum and the regulator's requirements are separate obligations that both apply. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the international curriculum, and KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab pupils and for Arabic as a first language. For non-Arab pupils, Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies are delivered in the school's licensed-curriculum language instead, and the two groups must be taught in separate classes.

faqs.question: What is the Bilingual Diploma and is it worth the extra work?
faqs.answer: It recognises a student who takes two languages at the studies-in-language-and-literature level rather than one plus a language acquisition subject, which for an Arabic first-language student in the UAE usually means Arabic A plus English A. Whether it is worth it depends on the destination list. For Gulf universities and for students who will work professionally in both languages it carries real weight. For a student applying to a quantitative degree where the offer is expressed in Higher Level grades, the extra reading load can cost more in points than the designation gains. Decide against published requirements, not on principle.

faqs.question: Our child has been in the mandatory Arabic stream since FS1 but has learned very little. What now?
faqs.answer: This is common and worth facing before the language acquisition decision rather than after. The mandatory stream carries no external examination in most years, so weak progress goes unchallenged until a course has to be chosen. Choose from assessed attainment rather than years attended: a student with real attainment can sit Arabic B, while one with attendance and little retention is better served by ab initio or another language the school timetables. Ask the school for the child's current level against the stream's own descriptors, in writing, before the option form is signed.

faqs.question: Does Arabic count towards the five subjects the Ministry of Education asks for?
faqs.answer: No. On the British track the requirement is five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. That exclusion matters in Year 9, because a student counting both towards the total will be two subjects short at the point of application. Verify the current rule through the Ministry's own channels before planning around it.

faqs.question: During Ramadan, can Arabic A sessions shift to a post-iftar slot and stay shorter?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is better to agree the change before the month starts than to improvise through it. School hours shorten, concentration patterns shift and the productive study window for most teenagers moves to the evening after iftar. Families with younger children often prefer the opposite and move sessions earlier. Shorter, more frequent sessions usually work better than long ones during the month. The week before Ramadan is also worth treating as a deadline for any coursework that would otherwise sit unfinished, because very little gets finished mid-month.

faqs.question: Are your Arabic tutors approved by KHDA to teach Islamic Education?
faqs.answer: No, and no private tutoring provider should claim that status. KHDA's requirement that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval applies to school staff in licensed schools, and a KHDA Educational Services Permit is a separate thing issued to training institutes with premises. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or licence from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. What a parent can reasonably do is ask the school to confirm the credential position for their child's own teacher, which is a question the regulator's rules make answerable.

faqs.question: Do you teach Arabic lessons at our home in Al Barsha?
faqs.answer: No. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered online, one to one, over live video, and IB Gram does not provide in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; those are offered only in India. For Arabic A specifically the online format is the reason a specialist is available at all, because Arabic A Literature at Higher Level is a narrow speciality and the pool of teachers who can teach it well is small. Choosing by subject and level rather than by driving distance is what makes the match work, particularly outside Dubai.

faqs.question: How much Arabic reading should be done over the summer before the final year?
faqs.answer: As much of the set-text load as possible, and this is the single highest-return decision available to an Arabic A student. The long summer between the two Diploma years is the only block of uninterrupted time in the course. Students who arrive in the final year having read everything spend term time on analysis practice, timed writing and oral rehearsal. Students who have not spend it on first reading, and then do their analysis practice in the weeks when the orals and internal deadlines land together. The difference usually shows in the comparative essay.

faqs.question: My daughter studied in English for ten years but we speak Arabic at home. Which course fits?
faqs.answer: This is the profile the placement review exists for, and the answer depends on reading rather than speaking. If she reads formal Standard Arabic at pace and can argue about an unfamiliar text, Arabic A is viable and worth pursuing for the Bilingual Diploma. If she reads slowly and writes with dialect features, Arabic A Higher Level would expose her for two years while Arabic B would reward her existing ability. One session with an unseen extract and a piece of written work settles it more reliably than a family discussion or a school default.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help prepare the individual oral if the recording is in three weeks?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the honesty boundary, and three weeks is enough to change the outcome. A tutor can test whether the chosen global issue is genuinely arguable across the two extracts, which is where most weak orals originate, explain how each criterion is applied, rehearse the oral under full time conditions and review the recording with the student. What a tutor cannot do is provide a script or prepared text for the student to deliver, because the oral has to be the student's own analysis. Structured rehearsal is what moves this component, not a better script.

faqs.question: Which English-medium subjects give Arabic first-language students the most trouble?
faqs.answer: Physics and chemistry first, because technical vocabulary met for the first time in English reads as a knowledge gap when it is a translation lag, and worded mathematics questions second, where the mathematics is secure and the multi-clause English costs time. Economics and business management follow, because both reward applying a named tool in precise academic English. In each case the fix is terminology and sentence structure taught explicitly, often by a bilingual tutor, rather than reteaching the subject. It is usually weeks of work rather than a year of tutoring.

faqs.question: How does the mandatory subject time affect the rest of the timetable?
faqs.answer: It reduces it. Mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, with weekly totals that must be met and an advisory minimum of 25 minutes for any single mandatory lesson, and those periods come out of the same week as everything else. A Dubai private school therefore has fewer periods available for the licensed curriculum than an equivalent school abroad. For an Arabic first-language student also taking Arabic A, the Arabic-medium share of the week is substantial, which is worth mapping before three Higher Levels are chosen.

faqs.question: What should we ask before paying for Arabic tutoring?
faqs.answer: Whether the tutor teaches the specific course and level, since Arabic A Literature, Arabic A Language and Literature, Arabic B and ab initio are four different jobs. Whether sessions are conducted in Standard Arabic. How work will be scored, and against which published criteria. Explicitly what the provider will not do with an oral, a Higher Level essay or an Extended Essay. The hourly rate in dirhams with the VAT position stated. And whether the tutor holds the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is granted free of charge for two years.

faqs.question: Is tutoring needed to pass the mandatory Arabic subjects?
faqs.answer: Usually not, and nobody should suggest otherwise. The mandatory subjects follow content approved by the Ministry of Education, and the guidelines prohibit the use of different or additional content without prior permission, so any support has to mean teaching the approved material well rather than supplying an alternative syllabus. Where a pupil is genuinely behind in reading Standard Arabic, targeted work on reading fluency helps across every Arabic-medium subject at once. Where the issue is engagement rather than ability, a conversation with the school is the better first step.

ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.closingHeading: Settle the course level, then teach the components
ib-tutor-for-arabic-speaking-students.closingBody: For Arabic-speaking families the largest single gain available is rarely more hours. It is confirming that the Arabic course level matches the student's reading rather than their speaking, and that the mandatory subject stream is the right one, because both decisions run for years once made. Tell us the exact course and level your child has been placed in, send a piece of written Arabic and the last report, and take a free trial lesson with a first-language specialist who will put an unseen extract in front of them. Lessons run online, one to one, in Gulf Standard Time, and move later during Ramadan by arrangement. If the placement is already right, that is what you will be told.

ib-tutor-for-indian-students.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below teach IB Diploma and MYP subjects to students who came through CBSE, ICSE or an Indian state board. Several have taught both systems, which is what makes the mapping work useful rather than theoretical.

intro.heading: The jump is not about ability. It is about what the marker rewards
paragraphs: Indian-curriculum schooling is the second largest curriculum group in Dubai's private sector, accounting for 26% of enrolment against 37% for UK-curriculum schools, 14% American and 7% International Baccalaureate, across 227 licensed schools and 387,441 pupils in 2024-25. Those proportions explain a pattern that repeats every September: a strong CBSE student enters DP1 at an IB school, works as hard as always, and receives a grade 4 in a subject where they used to score in the high eighties. The family concludes the child has slipped. Almost always, nothing has slipped.

What has changed is the thing being measured. A CBSE paper rewards a complete, accurate, well-presented answer to a question whose shape was predictable from the textbook. An IB paper rewards a response that does precisely what the command term asked, in the register the subject expects, with reasoning visible rather than implied. A student who writes everything they know scores well in one system and poorly in the other. That is a translation problem, and translation problems close in weeks once they are named.

The second shift is independence. CBSE and ICSE assess almost entirely through examinations set outside the school. The Diploma asks a sixteen-year-old to choose a research question, design an investigation, carry it out over months and write it up against published criteria, with internal deadlines set by their own school. Students arriving from a system where the syllabus told them what to do next find this genuinely disorienting, and the usual failure is not poor work but work started far too late.

The third is the grade scale itself. A one-to-seven subject grade built from criterion marks does not map onto a percentage, and the conversion is not linear. Parents who read a 5 as sixty-odd per cent and panic are misreading a scale on which a 5 is a solid, university-viable grade in a Higher Level subject. Before any tutoring is bought, it is worth understanding what the number means, because a surprising amount of the pressure Indian families put on Diploma students comes from a scale misread.

An IB tutor for indian students in the UAE is therefore doing three concrete jobs: mapping content coverage from the Indian board onto the IB subject guide, teaching the answer construction an IB examiner marks, and putting a realistic internal assessment schedule in place against the school's own deadlines. All three are finite. None of them is general tuition, and none of them requires the volume of hours families often assume.

Lessons are delivered online, one to one, over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not provide in-home visits anywhere in the UAE; those are offered only in India. For an Indian family in Sharjah or Ajman, where the specialist supply of Higher Level teachers is thinner than in Dubai, the online format is what makes a genuine subject specialist reachable at all.
