sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies on a Ras Al Khaimah timetable
paragraphs: Every family arriving into the northern emirates on an international curriculum meets the same surprise: the timetable is not only the curriculum the school is licensed to teach. Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies sit alongside it, and they are examined and reported on like any other subject.

The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations. In Dubai the Knowledge and Human Development Authority sets out the detail publicly, and its guidance is instructive for families anywhere in the country: Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies must be taught in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, with combined classes for both groups strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ.

That same guidance requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arab students in Islamic Education and in moral, social and cultural studies. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the advice is that no mandatory-subject lesson runs shorter than twenty-five minutes.

One constraint shapes how any tutor may work on these subjects: for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited. In practice that means a tutor supporting Arabic as an additional language works from the school's own material and the student's own exercise book, builds vocabulary and grammar through practice, and does not substitute an alternative syllabus. Families in Al Dhait and Al Qusaidat ask about this stream more often than families in the coastal communities, and it is one of the harder matches we make.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: the line a tutor does not cross
paragraphs: One site ranking in this market sells finished Internal Assessments. That is not a competitive difference of opinion; under IB rules it is malpractice, and the student carries the consequence. So it is worth setting out plainly what a tutor is for.

A tutor teaches, questions, models and gives feedback. The student is the sole author of every assessed piece: the Middle Years Personal Project, a Diploma internal assessment, the Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay, International GCSE coursework. A tutor may teach the criteria, work through an unrelated worked example, ask why a conclusion follows from the data, mark a practice question, and comment on a draft the student wrote. A tutor may not supply text to be submitted, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, or choose and develop the research question on the student's behalf.

The distinction is easier to hold in practice than it sounds, because it maps onto a simple test: after the session, could the student explain every sentence in their own document without looking at anything the tutor sent? If the answer is no, the line has been crossed. We tell tutors to work that way and we tell families to expect it, including when a deadline is close and the temptation is highest.

There is a second honesty point specific to the UAE. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff, as reported in the press, prohibit teachers from giving paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation permit carries a code of conduct that also bars serving students affiliated with the teacher's own school. We do not arrange for a child to be tutored privately by their own class teacher, anywhere in the country.

sections.heading: Online delivery for Al Hamra Village, stated plainly
paragraphs: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. There is no tutor who will arrive at a villa on the golf course or an apartment in Bab Al Bahr, and no UAE office or centre to visit either. Home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Saying that clearly on a page a parent reached by searching for a tutor in their own village is better than discovering it on a phone call.

What happens instead is a live one-to-one video lesson. The student joins from a laptop or tablet, the tutor shares a whiteboard, and the student's own exercise book, past paper or draft is on screen. Written work is photographed and uploaded, marked, annotated and returned. For sciences, the tutor works through the school's practical write-ups and data rather than running an experiment, which is the same thing a classroom teacher does when marking a lab report.

The argument for this format in Al Hamra Village is not that it is more convenient, although it is. It is that it changes who is available. A village family choosing from people willing to drive out from Al Nakheel on a weekday evening is choosing from a very short list. A village family choosing from specialists who teach that exact syllabus on Gulf Standard Time is choosing from a much longer one, and for Higher Level sciences or Economics that difference is the whole of the decision.

The honest limits are worth stating too. Online lessons need a reliable connection and a quiet room, which is harder in a shared apartment than in a villa. Younger students need a parent within earshot for the first few weeks. And a student who will not switch a camera on learns less than one who will, because a tutor who cannot see the working cannot correct it. We raise all three before the first paid lesson rather than after.

process.title: Tell us the campus, the board and the tier
process.description: Not just the subject. A Ras Al Khaimah student doing Physics might be on Cambridge 0625 Core, Cambridge Extended, Pearson 4PH1 or Diploma Standard Level, and those are four different courses. We ask for the school name, the syllabus code if you have it, and the last report.

process.title: A free first lesson with the matched tutor
process.description: The first lesson costs nothing and carries no obligation to continue. It is diagnostic: the tutor works through a topic the student finds hard and sends a short written note afterwards on what the actual gap is. If the match is wrong, we change the tutor rather than asking you to persist with it.

process.title: Fix a slot that survives the Al Hamra school run
process.description: We set the weekly time against your real afternoon, not an ideal one. For most village secondary students that lands between 17:00 and 19:00 Gulf Standard Time, with Friday afternoon available for longer sessions. The slot is held through holidays unless you ask us to pause it.

process.title: Work from marked papers, not from a syllabus checklist
process.description: Lessons are built around questions the student has actually got wrong. Written work is uploaded, marked against the published criteria or mark scheme, and returned annotated, so the next lesson starts from evidence rather than from a parent's impression of how things are going.

process.title: Review against the board's calendar, not the school term
process.description: Every six to eight weeks we check progress against what the exam series requires by that date, which for Cambridge candidates means entry deadlines and forecast grades as well as papers. If the plan needs more hours, we say so early enough for it to be a choice.

whyPoints.title: Distance stops being the constraint
whyPoints.description: The thing that limits a family in Al Hamra Village is not traffic but supply: how many people within reach have taught the exact syllabus. Teaching over video removes the drive-time filter entirely, and for Higher Level sciences and Economics that is the difference between a specialist and a generalist.

whyPoints.title: Coverage is disclosed before you pay
whyPoints.description: If no tutor teaching from inside the UAE covers the subject and level you need, we say so and offer the alternative rather than quietly filling the slot. No competitor in this market publishes a coverage limit, which is why so many families discover one after the first invoice.

whyPoints.title: The board and the tier are checked first
whyPoints.description: Cambridge and Pearson set different papers for the same subject name, and Cambridge Core caps the attainable grade. A tutor who starts teaching before confirming which the school entered the student for can spend a whole term preparing material the student will never sit.

whyPoints.title: Figures are sourced, not invented
whyPoints.description: Every AED rate on this page is attributed to the competitor or market survey that published it, with the tier it applies to. We publish no satisfaction percentage, no star rating and no student headcount, because none of those could be produced with a method and a date behind them.

whyPoints.title: The student stays the author
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach the assessment criteria, mark practice work and comment on the student's own drafts. They do not supply text for submission or develop a research question on a student's behalf, and we say why: under IB rules the consequence of that help falls on the student, not the tutor.

whyPoints.title: A timetable that holds through Ramadan and travel
whyPoints.description: Lesson times are re-based for Ramadan and for part-year households rather than suspended, with the same tutor either side. For a student in the final year of a two-year course, continuity through those weeks is worth more than any individual lesson in them.

faqs.question: Can a family living in Al Hamra Village actually get a Higher Level subject specialist?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the main reason to use a remote service here rather than a local one. The limit in Ras Al Khaimah is not traffic, it is how few people within driving distance have taught a specific Higher Level syllabus. Teaching over live video removes the drive-time filter, so the pool becomes everyone who teaches that course on Gulf Standard Time. For Higher Level Chemistry, Physics, Economics and Business Management the match usually takes one to three weeks, and we tell you that date before you pay rather than after.

faqs.question: What time can a lesson realistically start if my child is schooled in Al Nakheel?
faqs.answer: Plan for 17:00 at the earliest and 17:30 if you want a slot that survives a bad traffic day. The run from Al Nakheel or Khuzam back to Al Hamra Village takes twenty-five to thirty-five minutes, and once food and a sibling pickup are factored in, a 16:00 lesson becomes a weekly negotiation. Families with a parent commuting from Dubai usually settle on 18:30 or 19:00. Friday afternoon, after the early school finish, is the best ninety-minute window in the week for extended writing or coursework.

faqs.question: Does anyone come to our villa in Al Hamra Village for the lesson?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE, and there is no office or centre in the country to visit either. Home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Every UAE lesson is one-to-one over live video, with a shared whiteboard and the student's own exercise book, past paper or draft on screen. Written work is photographed, uploaded, marked and returned annotated. We state this before a first lesson is booked because it is a genuine difference and not something to find out on a phone call.

faqs.question: Which schools do children from Al Hamra Village usually attend?
faqs.answer: Three clusters cover almost all of them. There is provision inside or immediately beside the community in the Al Hamra and Al Jazirah Al Hamra area, which gives the shortest run in the emirate. There is the larger concentration in Al Nakheel, serving families from across Ras Al Khaimah, and there is Khuzam inland, which includes senior-school and IB continuum places. Schools are named on this page as context for the local education map only; IB Gram has no affiliation or partnership with any of them, and we confirm the campus, board and tier before matching a tutor.

faqs.question: We spend part of the year away from the village - can lessons follow us?
faqs.answer: That is a standard pattern here and we schedule for it rather than around it. The tutor stays the same and the clock is re-based to wherever the family is, so a 17:30 Gulf Standard Time slot becomes whatever the local equivalent is. We ask for travel weeks in advance so the topic order can be re-sequenced, and marked work sits in a shared folder so nothing is lost in the move. Families who stop for eight weeks and restart usually spend more over a two-year course, because re-diagnosis costs lesson time.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates my child's school if we live in Al Hamra Village?
faqs.answer: The Ras Al Khaimah Department of Knowledge, which the UAE government describes as regulating private education in the emirate. Alongside Sharjah's authority it also approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, which is a wider remit than inspection alone. Underneath that sits a federal baseline: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. IB Gram is not approved or licensed by any of these bodies and does not claim to be.

faqs.question: Our son sits Cambridge International GCSE at a Ras Al Khaimah centre - when does the entry close?
faqs.answer: Much earlier than most families expect, and the school makes the entry rather than the parent. For the March 2027 series Cambridge publishes final entries due on 27 November 2026, forecast grades due 27 February 2027 and the exam period running 3 February to 4 March 2027. Every centre is also allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct zone timetable and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong version. Check both with the school in writing.

faqs.question: Is private tuition cheaper in Ras Al Khaimah than it is in Dubai?
faqs.answer: For generalist work, usually a little. For genuine specialists, no. Published market figures put budget online tutoring at roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, qualified subject tutors at AED 150 to 300, and IB or IGCSE specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, with one provider quoting AED 650. Those bands do not drop in the northern emirates, because the scarcity that sets the price is national rather than local. These are market rates published by other providers, not an IB Gram price list, and the free first lesson is where our own pricing conversation starts.

faqs.question: My daughter is one of very few in the emirate taking Economics Higher Level - is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It is a supply problem, not a teaching one, and it is the single most common reason families this far north contact us. Economics and Business Management are the thinnest subjects in our Ras Al Khaimah coverage, with a typical match taking one to three weeks. The work itself is well-defined: diagram accuracy is where most marks are lost, so lessons concentrate on labelled axes, shift arrows and the written link between the diagram and the argument, practised on unseen questions rather than on notes she already has.

faqs.question: Does my child still take Arabic if the school teaches a British curriculum?
faqs.answer: Yes. The federal position is that private schools must cover Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies regardless of the international curriculum they are licensed to teach. Dubai's authority publishes the clearest detail, and it is instructive nationally: Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies must run as separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, with combined classes strictly prohibited because expectations and language of instruction differ. For mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, so a tutor works from the school's own material.

faqs.question: What will the Ministry of Education want to see when my child applies to a UAE university?
faqs.answer: For the British track the published requirement is five accredited subjects at International GCSE or GCSE with a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count of five, plus either one accredited Advanced Level subject at grade E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. One ranking competitor states six subjects are required, which does not match the published rule. Equivalency is a process the Ministry runs, not something a tutoring service performs, so verify the current requirement on the Ministry's own pages.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark my son's past papers and send them back with comments?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is most of what a useful lesson is built on. The student photographs completed work, uploads it, and the tutor marks it against the published mark scheme or assessment criteria, annotates where marks were lost and returns it before the next session. Lessons then start from evidence rather than from an impression. What we do not do is reproduce or supply board past papers, mark schemes or syllabus documents as downloads; those belong to Cambridge, Pearson and the IB, and we link the official source instead.

faqs.question: What is a tutor allowed to help with on a Personal Project or an internal assessment?
faqs.answer: A tutor may teach the published criteria, model the thinking on an unrelated example, ask why a conclusion follows from the data, and comment on a draft the student has already written. A tutor may not supply text for submission, rewrite a paragraph into its final form, or choose and develop the research question for the student. The working test is simple: after the session, could the student explain every sentence in their own document without looking at anything the tutor sent? If not, the line has been crossed, and the consequence under IB rules falls on the student.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting lessons halfway through a term?
faqs.answer: Often it is the best time, particularly for a household that has just arrived into Bab Al Bahr or Al Hamra Views mid-year. A student joining a Cambridge or Pearson course part way through has a defined backlog, and the first two sessions are spent auditing the syllabus against what has actually been taught. That produces a list of missed topics, which is a much better plan than general revision. Two shorter lessons a week while the gap closes, dropping to one once it has, is the pattern that works.

faqs.question: Do lessons carry on during Ramadan?
faqs.answer: They carry on, but the time moves. School days shorten and the late afternoon stops working for most Ras Al Khaimah households, so the whole emirate's timetable shifts to post-Iftar slots agreed before the month begins. The tutor stays the same throughout, which matters more than the hour itself for a student in the second year of a two-year course. Families who prefer to pause can reserve the slot for a stated number of weeks instead, and we would rather agree that in advance than lose a month to cancellations.

ras-al-khaimah/al-hamra-village.closingHeading: Start with one free lesson and a straight answer about availability
ras-al-khaimah/al-hamra-village.closingBody: If you are in Al Hamra Village, Mina Al Arab or Al Marjan Island, tell us the campus, the board, the tier and the subject, and we will tell you whether a specialist is available now, in a week, or in three. The first lesson is free and carries no obligation to continue, and it ends with a written note on what the real gap is rather than a sales call. Lessons are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, timed around your actual school run, and the tutor stays the same through Ramadan and through travel. If we cannot cover the subject you need on the timeline you need it, we will say so.

ras-al-khaimah/al-mamourah.tutorsIntro: The tutors below work across the primary and middle years as well as the examination stages. For a younger child, matching is about pace and manner as much as subject knowledge, which is what the trial lesson is for.

intro.heading: The useful questions here are about Year 4, not Year 11
paragraphs: Al Mamourah sits on the northern side of the Ras Al Khaimah creek, next to Al Qusaidat, a residential neighbourhood of established villas and low-rise apartment blocks with a settled population and a lot of young children. It is not a district people pass through. Families move here and stay, which means the schooling conversation here starts early and runs long, often across three children spaced several years apart.

The enquiries that arrive from this neighbourhood are younger than anywhere else in the emirate. A Year 3 child who reads aloud haltingly. A Year 5 child who can do mental arithmetic and cannot set out written working. A Year 7 child whose first Middle Years Programme report has arrived with four letters and a number on it and nobody at home knows what any of them mean. A Year 9 family wondering whether to start now or wait until the exam years.

Those are better questions than the ones that arrive in February of Year 11, and they deserve different answers. Some of them deserve the answer that no tutoring is needed yet, which is not a popular thing for a tutoring page to say and is often true. A Year 2 child who is behind on reading needs twenty minutes a day with a parent and a library ticket far more than a paid session, and a family told otherwise is being sold something.

Where early support genuinely changes an outcome is narrower and more specific than the market implies. Reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina are measurable in minutes, they predict almost everything that follows, and they respond quickly to short frequent practice. Those three are worth attention at primary. Most other things at that age are better left to the school and to time.

The middle years are different again, because the assessment system is opaque to parents arriving from any examination-led background. A Middle Years Programme grade is built from four criteria, each marked out of eight, and the single reported number hides which of the four is weak. That is the most useful thing a family in this district can learn to read, and the sections below set it out subject group by subject group.

Tuition for Al Mamourah families is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video, with shorter sessions for younger children. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address; home visits are a service offered only in India. Private schools in this emirate are regulated by the Department of Knowledge, which approves curricula, programmes, courses, activities, assessment methods and tuition fees. That is a different authority from Dubai's KHDA, so advice written for Dubai parents about reporting, assessment or inspection does not transfer directly to a school on this side of the creek.

ras-al-khaimah/al-mamourah.programmesIntro: The four stages below are what a family in this district works through over ten or twelve years. The early ones are measured in skills; the later ones in criteria and then in marks.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, transdisciplinary and unexamined, organised around units of inquiry rather than subject syllabuses. Reporting is descriptive rather than numerical in most schools, which is excellent for understanding a child's engagement and poor for answering whether they are behind.
programmes.countryNote: The practical consequence for an Al Mamourah family is that you have to ask for numbers the report does not give you. Reading age, a standardised score if the school uses one, and whether number facts are automatic. All three are answerable by a class teacher in a five-minute conversation, and none of them normally appears on a PYP report.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria marked out of eight, with the total converted to a 1-7 grade using published boundaries. An optional eAssessment at the end of MYP 5 leads to a formal certificate through on-screen examinations and ePortfolios.
programmes.countryNote: This is where families in this district have the least information and the school has the most. A 5 is a comfortable-looking number that can hide a weak criterion, and in practice a student strong on knowledge and weak on communicating is heading for exactly the mark losses that surface in a Diploma or IGCSE paper three years later. Ask which criterion the grade is built from, every reporting cycle.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined terminally, with Cambridge running June and November series and Pearson running May/June and November. Tiered entries in some subjects cap the available grade, and the tier decision is taken in Year 10.
programmes.countryNote: For a family that has been in the MYP, the move into IGCSE is a change of assessment culture rather than content. Students assessed against criteria for four years meet published mark schemes, command terms and timed papers for the first time, and the shock is in the format. A summer on technique rather than new content is the usual bridge.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internally assessed work carries a real share of each subject grade and terminal papers are sat in the May session at almost every UAE school.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is offered at the coastal campuses rather than in the city, so a northern family choosing it is choosing a long daily journey. That is worth knowing a decade early, because it is one of the factors families here weigh when deciding which primary school to start a child in.

ras-al-khaimah/al-mamourah.subjectsIntro: At primary and middle-years level the useful unit is a skill rather than a subject. The list below pairs each subject with the specific thing worth measuring at this district's typical age range.

subjects.name: Reading and comprehension (primary)
subjects.description: Fluency first, comprehension second. A child who decodes slowly cannot hold a sentence's meaning long enough to answer a question about it, so comprehension work on a weak decoder produces frustration. Ten minutes of reading aloud daily beats an hour a week.

subjects.name: Written stamina (primary)
subjects.description: The ability to sustain a written paragraph, which is separate from having ideas. Children who speak fluently and write three lines are not weak at the subject; they are untrained at writing at length. Twenty minutes of timed writing twice a week changes it.

subjects.name: Number facts and mental arithmetic
subjects.description: Automatic recall of tables, number bonds and doubles. A child computing 7 times 8 from scratch has no working memory left for the problem the question is actually about, which is why arithmetic recall predicts secondary mathematics performance so strongly.

subjects.name: Mathematics (lower secondary)
subjects.description: Fractions, negative numbers, index laws and rearranging formulae. These four are the weaknesses that resurface in a Year 11 mock three years later, and they are considerably cheaper to fix at thirteen than at sixteen.

subjects.name: MYP Mathematics
subjects.description: Assessed against knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Students often score well on the first and poorly on communicating, which is a presentation and notation habit rather than a mathematical weakness.

subjects.name: MYP Sciences
subjects.description: Assessed against knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The design and evaluation criteria are where marks go missing, and they are the direct ancestors of IGCSE practical questions.

subjects.name: MYP Language and Literature
subjects.description: Assessed against analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. Organizing is the criterion most often weak and the one that most directly predicts Diploma paper performance, because it is paragraph architecture under another name.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Reading at speed and the summary task separate the grades later, and both are built on reading volume now. The speaking endorsement arrangements differ between the two codes, which matters only at entry but matters absolutely then.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools from the early years regardless of the licensed curriculum, taught to prescribed content. Starting it properly in primary is far easier than repairing it in Year 9, and progress comes from short frequent practice.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with separate streams for Arab and non-Arab students and different languages of instruction. Content is prescribed, so support works within the school's own scheme.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: Included here because the Year 10 tier decision is shaped by Years 7 to 9. A student whose arithmetic recall and algebraic fluency are secure at thirteen is entered for the higher tier at fifteen; one whose are not often is not.

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Mamourah, and why the questions start younger
paragraphs: This is a neighbourhood people settle in rather than pass through. The housing is established, the villas have been in the same families for years, and the demographic skews towards households with two or three children spread across primary and the middle years. There is no large transient expatriate population here of the kind that drives short-term exam-year enquiries in the Dubai communities.

That changes what parents want to know. A family three years into a school is not asking whether their child can be rescued before May; they are asking whether something they have noticed is normal. The reading that is slower than a cousin's. The written work that is always three lines shorter than the task asked for. The report that says the child is a confident learner and gives no indication of whether they are behind.

Those enquiries are more valuable to answer honestly than exam-year ones, because the margin for action is years rather than weeks. They are also where a tutoring market is most likely to oversell, since an anxious parent of a seven-year-old is an easy sale and nobody will ever be able to prove the sessions were unnecessary.

The position taken on this page is narrow deliberately. Three things are worth measuring and supporting at primary: reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina. In the middle years, one thing is worth understanding: which of the four criteria behind a grade is weak. Everything else at these ages is usually better served by the school, by time, and by twenty minutes a day at home.

sections.heading: The age ladder: what is worth supporting, stage by stage
paragraphs: Tutoring is not a single product applied at different ages. What is useful at seven and what is useful at fifteen have almost nothing in common, and a provider that offers the same weekly hour across the range is not thinking about the difference. The honest version is a ladder, where each rung has its own measurement, its own session length and its own list of things to ignore.

At the bottom of the ladder the work is mechanical and the gains are fast. Reading fluency and number-fact recall are both trainable with short daily repetition, and both can be measured well enough at home to tell whether anything is changing. A parent can run most of it. A tutor is useful where a child has stopped cooperating with a parent on the subject, which happens more often than families admit and is a perfectly good reason to bring in someone else.

In the middle of the ladder the work becomes about process: setting out written mathematics, organising a paragraph, planning before writing. This is where the MYP criteria live, and where most of the marks that go missing at sixteen are actually lost. It is also the least glamorous thing to pay for, because the child already knows the content and is losing marks on presentation.

At the top the work is technique against a published mark scheme, and the measurement is a marked paper. The useful point about the ladder is that each rung is cheaper than the one above it. A written-stamina problem fixed in Year 4 costs a fraction of the same problem addressed as an extended-response weakness in Year 11, and that is the strongest argument for starting early that does not involve frightening anybody.

sections.heading: Reading age and number facts: the two measurements that predict everything
paragraphs: Two numbers tell a parent more about a primary child's academic future than any report. The first is reading age, which schools in this emirate commonly measure with a standardised test and rarely volunteer unless asked. The second is whether number facts are automatic, which is not formally measured at all and can be checked at the kitchen table in five minutes.

Reading age matters because it gates everything taught through text, which by Year 5 is almost everything. A child reading two years below their chronological age is not slow at science; they are spending their working memory on decoding the question. The repair is volume: reading aloud daily, at a level where they stumble occasionally rather than constantly, for ten to fifteen minutes. It works, and it takes months rather than weeks.

Number-fact automaticity matters for the same reason in a different register. A child who computes seven times eight from scratch has nothing left for the problem the question was about, which is why arithmetic recall predicts secondary mathematics so strongly. The test is to ask twenty mixed facts at conversational speed and count the hesitations. More than a handful and recall is not automatic.

The reason to measure both now rather than later is cost, not alarm. Both are cheap to fix at eight and expensive to work around at fifteen, where they present as a general weakness in a subject rather than as a specific mechanical gap. The table below sets out how to test each, what a weak result looks like, and what actually changes it. Most of the column on the right is work a parent can do; a tutor is for the cases where that has stopped working.

sections.heading: How to read a Middle Years Programme grade
paragraphs: This is the single most useful thing a family in this district can learn, and almost nobody explains it. An MYP subject grade is not a mark out of a hundred converted to a scale. It is built from four criteria, each marked out of eight by the teacher against published descriptors, with the total converted to a 1-7 grade using boundaries the IB publishes. The reported number therefore averages four quite different judgements.

That averaging is what hides a problem. A student scoring well on the knowledge criterion and poorly on the communication criterion can land on a comfortable 5, and a parent reading only the 5 will conclude everything is fine. In practice that profile is a warning: communicating and organising are the direct ancestors of extended-response marks at IGCSE and paper marks in the Diploma, and a weakness there compounds for years while the overall grade looks acceptable.

The criterion names differ by subject group, which is why a single explanation does not work. In mathematics they cover knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In the sciences they cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In language and literature they cover analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. Confirm the current set with your child's school, because the frameworks are periodically revised.

The question to ask at every reporting cycle is therefore specific: which criterion is this grade weakest on, and what would the next band up require. A class teacher can answer that in two minutes, and the answer tells a family exactly what to work on. It also prevents the most common and most wasteful response to a middling MYP grade, which is generic extra content work in a subject where the content was never the problem.

sections.heading: Year 6 into Year 7: the step families underestimate
paragraphs: The move into Year 7 is treated as a pastoral event, with a transition day and a tour of the building, and the academic change is barely discussed. It is substantial. A child goes from one teacher who knows them to eight or nine who do not, from one classroom to a timetable, from homework set by a familiar adult to homework set by subject in a diary nobody checks at the same level of detail.

The academic consequences are predictable. Work that was previously scaffolded now arrives with less structure. Notes have to be kept in a form the child can find again. Deadlines arrive from several directions at once. And for an MYP student, assessment switches from descriptive comment to criterion marking, which nobody explains to an eleven-year-old in terms they can act on.

The children who struggle in Year 7 are frequently not the academically weakest. They are the ones whose organisation was previously provided by an adult and who now have to supply it themselves. That is a learnable skill and the best time to teach it is the summer before, not the November after a first difficult report.

The practical content of a transition block is unglamorous: how to keep notes so they can be retrieved, how to read a task and identify what is actually being asked, how to plan a piece of writing before starting it, and how to work for thirty minutes without being prompted. The table lists what changes and what to do about each. None of it is content, which is why schools rarely have room for it.

sections.heading: MYP 5 into the Diploma, or into Year 10 IGCSE
paragraphs: At the top of the Middle Years Programme a family in this district faces one of two moves, and both involve the same underlying change: from criterion assessment to a published mark scheme. A student who has spent four or five years being marked against descriptors meets command terms, method marks and timed papers, often for the first time, and the difficulty is format rather than content.

Into Year 10 IGCSE the gap is mainly technique. Students are usually content-ready and unprepared for the specific demands of a mark scheme: showing method to earn method marks, answering to the depth the command term requires, and working at the pace a full paper demands. A term of timed practice with real marking generally closes it, and it is far better done in Year 10 than discovered in a Year 11 mock.

Into the Diploma the gap is wider and includes independence. Internal assessments the student designs themselves, a 4,000-word Extended Essay with a supervisor rather than a teacher, Theory of Knowledge with no content to revise, and CAS commitments on top. MYP's emphasis on inquiry prepares students philosophically for this and does not prepare them for the volume or the deadline management.

There is also the optional MYP eAssessment to consider, which leads to a formal certificate through on-screen examinations and ePortfolios at the end of MYP 5. Where a school offers it, it gives a student their first experience of an externally assessed timed examination, which has real value as preparation regardless of the result. Ask the school whether it is offered and what it involves, since not every campus runs it.

sections.heading: What early support costs, and when to wait
paragraphs: No rate table has been published for Ras Al Khaimah, so every AED figure in this market comes from a Dubai source. The bands below carry the provider who publishes them and should be read as a ceiling rather than a local quote. For primary-age work the relevant point is that the cheapest band is usually appropriate, which is the opposite of the advice that applies at Higher Level.

Primary reading and number-fact work does not need a subject specialist. It needs someone patient, consistent and willing to do the same short thing twice a week for a term, which is the budget tier of this market rather than the specialist tier. Paying specialist rates for tables practice is a straightforward waste, and any provider steering a family there for a Year 3 child is selling rather than advising.

The middle years sit in the middle band, because criterion work needs someone who knows the framework and can read a descriptor properly. The specialist tier becomes relevant at IGCSE and Diploma level, where board-specific knowledge and marking against a published scheme are what is being bought.

And sometimes the answer is to wait. A Year 1 child who is behind on reading needs daily reading at home and a conversation with the class teacher, not a paid arrangement. A Year 8 child with a dip in one subject after a change of teacher usually needs a term to settle. A family that is told to wait and comes back a year later with a clearer picture has lost nothing, and the honest answer costs a provider a sale, which is exactly why it is worth hearing.

sections.heading: Arabic and the mandatory subjects from the first year of school
paragraphs: Families in this district often reach Year 9 and discover that Arabic has quietly become a problem. It is on the timetable from the early years in every UAE private school regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and the federal position is explicit: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations.

The reason it drifts is that it is nobody's priority. It is not examined externally in the early years, it does not appear on a university application, and a child who is behind in it can coast for several years without consequence. The consequence arrives later, as a subject that has to be endured rather than studied, and in some cases as a complication at the point of equivalency, where Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five IGCSE subjects the Ministry requires on the British track.

The structural rules are worth knowing because they shape what support can look like. KHDA's published guidelines for Dubai schools set out the clearest version: separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes for both groups strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Arabic as a first language and for Islamic Education for Arab students.

One constraint applies absolutely. For the mandatory subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is prohibited, so any support has to work inside the school's own prescribed scheme rather than importing material from elsewhere. That makes these sessions unlike any other: the task is fluency and confidence within a fixed syllabus. Starting that in primary, with short frequent practice, is far easier than attempting it in Year 9.

process.title: Ask the school for the numbers first
process.description: Reading age or standardised score, and whether number facts are automatic. Neither normally appears on a primary report and both are answerable in a five-minute conversation. Those two figures determine whether anything is needed at all, which is the question worth settling before any arrangement.

process.title: For the middle years, ask which criterion is weak
process.description: An MYP grade averages four criteria marked out of eight. Ask the subject teacher which one the grade is weakest on and what the next band up would require. That turns a middling number into a specific target, usually a writing or presentation habit rather than missing content.

process.title: Pick one target, not a subject
process.description: Reading fluency, number facts, written stamina, or one named MYP criterion. Younger children make visible progress on one thing at a time and almost none on a general plan to improve at a subject, which is unmeasurable and therefore unreviewable.

process.title: Short sessions, more often
process.description: Twenty minutes twice a week at Years 1 and 2, rising to forty by Year 6. Frequency does the work at this age. A single hour-long weekly session for a young child produces perhaps twenty minutes of useful attention and costs three times as much per useful minute.

process.title: Review in six weeks against the same measurement
process.description: Retake the measurement that started the arrangement: the same reading passage, the same twenty number facts, the same timed paragraph. If it has not moved, the approach changes. Six weeks is long enough to show movement and short enough not to waste a term.

whyPoints.title: An honest answer about whether anything is needed
whyPoints.description: Some enquiries about young children should end with a recommendation to read daily and speak to the class teacher. A provider that never says that is not advising. Families told to wait and who return a year later with a clearer picture have lost nothing.

whyPoints.title: Measurable targets at primary age
whyPoints.description: Reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina are testable in minutes and respond to short frequent practice. Sessions are built around one of them at a time, with the same measurement retaken after six weeks so progress is visible rather than asserted.

whyPoints.title: The MYP framework explained properly
whyPoints.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight, converted to a 1-7 grade. Work targets the specific weak criterion read from the school's own breakdown, which is almost always communicating or organising rather than knowledge.

whyPoints.title: Session length set by age, not by convention
whyPoints.description: Twenty minutes for a Year 1 child, forty by Year 6, sixty in the middle years, seventy-five to ninety in an exam year. Selling a standard hour to a seven-year-old is selling attention the child does not have.

whyPoints.title: The right tier for the job
whyPoints.description: Primary reading and tables work does not need a Higher Level specialist, and paying specialist rates for it is waste. The specialist tier becomes relevant at IGCSE and Diploma level, where board-specific knowledge and marking against a published scheme are what is being bought.

whyPoints.title: Plain about what IB Gram is
whyPoints.description: An independent tutor-matching platform with no UAE premises and no accreditation from the Department of Knowledge, KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson. Schools named on this page are local context only.

faqs.question: At what age does tutoring actually start being useful?
faqs.answer: It depends on what for. From about Year 3, three things respond well to short frequent sessions: reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina. Below that, a child who is behind on reading usually needs daily reading at home and a conversation with the class teacher rather than a paid arrangement. From Year 7 the useful work shifts to process, such as organising written work, and from Year 10 to technique against a published mark scheme. Each stage needs a different session length and a different kind of tutor.

faqs.question: How do I find out my child's reading age?
faqs.answer: Ask the school. Most schools in this emirate use a standardised reading test at least annually and hold a score that does not appear on the report, and a class teacher will share it if asked directly. You can also check fluency yourself in five minutes: listen to one page read aloud and note whether your child stumbles frequently, reads without expression or loses their place. A child reading two or more years below their chronological age is spending their working memory on decoding rather than on meaning.

faqs.question: What do the four MYP criteria actually mean?
faqs.answer: Each MYP subject is assessed against four named criteria, each marked out of eight, with the total converted to a 1-7 grade. The names differ by subject group. In mathematics they cover knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In the sciences, knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In language and literature, analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. Confirm the current set with your school, since the frameworks are periodically revised.

faqs.question: My son gets 5s in the MYP. Is that a good result?
faqs.answer: It is a comfortable-looking number that can hide a problem, which is why the useful question is which criterion the 5 is built from. A student strong on knowing and understanding and weak on communicating averages to a reassuring grade while carrying exactly the weakness that costs method and extended-response marks at IGCSE and in Diploma papers. Ask the subject teacher which criterion is weakest and what the next band up would require. That converts a 5 into a specific, workable target.

faqs.question: Is the MYP eAssessment worth sitting?
faqs.answer: Where a school offers it, there is a real argument for it beyond the certificate. It is an externally assessed set of on-screen examinations and ePortfolios at the end of MYP 5, and for many students it is their first experience of working to time under external assessment conditions. That experience has value as preparation for IGCSE or Diploma papers regardless of the outcome. Not every campus runs it, so ask the school whether it is offered, which subjects are included and what the timetable looks like.

faqs.question: What actually changes academically between Year 6 and Year 7?
faqs.answer: One teacher becomes eight or nine, so nobody sees the whole child. Homework arrives by subject and deadlines collide. Tasks come with less structure than before. Notes become the student's own record, and revision two years later depends on them. For MYP students, assessment switches from descriptive comment to criterion marks. The children who struggle are often not the weakest academically but the ones whose organisation was previously supplied by an adult, and that is a learnable skill best taught the summer before.

faqs.question: Should a Year 5 child have help with homework each week?
faqs.answer: Supervision at home, yes; a paid weekly session aimed at homework, usually not. Homework help tends to produce completed homework rather than an improved child, because the adult does the hard thinking at the moment the child should be doing it. If there is a real underlying gap, identify it and work on that directly: reading fluency, number facts or written stamina, measured at the start and retested after six weeks. That is a target you can judge; finished homework is not.

faqs.question: How long should a session be for a Year 3 child?
faqs.answer: Thirty minutes, twice a week, is the shape that works. Frequency does the work at this age, not duration. A full hour for an eight-year-old yields perhaps twenty minutes of genuine attention and costs three times as much per useful minute. The session should also set something short for the days in between, for a parent to oversee, because two sessions a week plus five days of nothing produces far less than two sessions plus ten minutes daily.

faqs.question: Does my child need Arabic support in primary school?
faqs.answer: If they are behind, starting now is far easier than repairing it in Year 9, which is when most families in this district notice. Arabic is on the timetable from the early years in every UAE private school regardless of the licensed curriculum, and the federal baseline covers Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies. Because the content is prescribed, support must work inside the school's own scheme rather than importing material, and additional or substituted content requires prior Ministry permission. Short frequent practice is what works.

faqs.question: Would it be better to wait until Year 10 before paying for anything?
faqs.answer: For subject content, often yes. For the three primary measurements and for MYP criterion habits, waiting is expensive. A written-stamina problem fixed in Year 4 costs a fraction of the same problem met in Year 11 as a weakness in extended responses, where it presents as a general subject difficulty and takes a term to shift. The distinction worth holding is between content, which the curriculum will cover anyway, and mechanical skills, which compound quietly if nobody addresses them.

faqs.question: What does early support cost for a family in Al Mamourah?
faqs.answer: Less than exam-year work, because it does not need a specialist. No rate table is published for this emirate, so the figures are Dubai ones: budget online tuition is published at AED 45-150 an hour and qualified subject tutors at AED 150-300, with specialists at AED 200-450 or more. Primary reading and number-fact work belongs in the lowest band, because what it needs is patience and consistency rather than board-specific expertise. Paying specialist rates for tables practice is a straightforward waste.

faqs.question: How do we know whether number facts are secure?
faqs.answer: Ask twenty mixed facts at conversational speed and count the hesitations. Tables, number bonds and doubles, jumbled rather than in order. More than a handful of pauses means recall is not automatic, and that matters more than it sounds: a child computing seven times eight from scratch has no working memory left for the problem the question was actually about. Two minutes of daily mixed drilling fixes it within a term, and it is the cheapest intervention available at this age.

faqs.question: My daughter talks about a topic fluently but writes three lines. What is that?
faqs.answer: Written stamina, and it is a separate skill from having ideas. Children who can explain something aloud and cannot sustain it on paper are not weak at the subject; they are untrained at writing at length, and that trains quickly. Twenty minutes of timed writing twice a week on familiar topics, with the only target being length and then structure, changes it within a term. Left alone it reappears at sixteen as mid-band extended responses, which is a far slower repair.

faqs.question: Can a primary child concentrate during a video lesson?
faqs.answer: For twenty to thirty minutes, yes, with two conditions. The session has to be short and highly structured, with the child writing or reading aloud rather than listening, and a parent should be nearby for the first few sessions to settle the routine rather than to participate. Headphones help. What does not work is an hour-long session where a young child is expected to watch and listen, which is the format that gives video lessons a poor reputation at this age.

faqs.question: When should we start thinking about the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Earlier than you would expect, because in this emirate it is partly a geography decision. The IB continuum and the Diploma sit at the coastal campuses rather than in the city, so a northern family choosing that route is choosing a long daily journey from the first year of school onwards. The academic decisions, subject choices and route comparisons belong in Year 10. The school decision that makes those options available belongs much earlier, and it is worth asking the question before a child starts primary.

ras-al-khaimah/al-mamourah.closingHeading: Start with two numbers and one criterion
ras-al-khaimah/al-mamourah.closingBody: For a younger child in Al Mamourah, the useful first step costs nothing: ask the school for a reading age, check twenty number facts at the kitchen table, and ask which MYP criterion a grade is weakest on. Send us those three answers and we will tell you honestly whether anything is needed yet, and if it is, what one target to work on and how long it should take. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, in sessions sized for the child's age rather than a standard hour.

intro.heading: Covered in class is not the same as secure in the student
paragraphs: Al Marjan Island is four reclaimed fronds off the Ras Al Khaimah coast, a mix of apartment towers, hotel residences and villa plots, connected to the mainland by a single causeway. Children here attend the RAK Academy campuses at Al Hamra and Khuzam, the British and Indian curriculum schools around the city, and in a smaller number of cases campuses in Sharjah or Umm Al Quwain. Whichever school they attend, the same conversation happens in February of an exam year.

The school reports that the syllabus has been delivered. The teacher is not wrong: the content has been taught, the practicals have been run, the mock has been sat. And yet the grade sits two bands below the prediction. The reason is almost never that something was skipped. It is that a syllabus delivered to a set of twenty-odd students at the pace the scheme of work demands leaves a substantial amount of consolidation to be done by each student alone, and nobody has told the student how much.

The numbers are worth stating plainly. An IGCSE subject typically receives three to four taught periods a week. The content volume in Cambridge Biology 0610 or Chemistry 0620 assumes the student is also revisiting, practising and self-testing outside those periods. At Diploma level the imbalance is larger still: a Higher Level subject carries 240 recommended teaching hours over two years, and the internal assessment, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge are timetabled thinly or not at all in many schools.

That unscheduled work is where grades are made and lost. A student who reads notes rather than answering questions will pass and will not reach the top bands. A student who never sits a full paper to time will lose marks to pacing rather than to knowledge. A student who starts an internal assessment in the term it is due will produce something adequate rather than something strong. None of these failures looks like a knowledge problem in class, which is why the school report rarely predicts them.

The sections below put numbers on the gap: taught hours against expected independent hours by stage, the components schools mark internally and those they do not, the internal assessment calendar most schools never hand out in full, and where marks actually disappear between a mock and a real paper. Tuition for Al Marjan Island families is delivered as one-to-one lessons over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a UAE address, and home visits are offered only in India.

One structural note. Private schools in Ras Al Khaimah are regulated by the emirate's Department of Knowledge, which approves curricula, programmes, courses, activities, assessment methods and tuition fees. Guidance written for Dubai families under KHDA does not transfer directly, so a question about how a school assesses or reports belongs with the Department of Knowledge and with the school itself.

ras-al-khaimah/al-marjan-island.programmesIntro: Three programmes dominate on this coast, and each leaves a different kind of gap. The Diploma leaves the internally assessed components under-supported; IGCSE leaves practice volume to the student; MYP leaves parents without a clear measure at all.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. Roughly a fifth to a quarter of most subject grades comes from internally assessed work completed across DP1 and DP2. The terminal papers are sat in the May session for almost every UAE school.
programmes.countryNote: The under-supported part of the Diploma in Ras Al Khaimah is the core. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay are usually given a supervisor and a handful of meetings rather than a taught course, and on a small campus the supervisor may not be a specialist in the student's chosen area. An Al Marjan Island student should assume the research question and the structure are their own responsibility from the outset.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined terminally, with Cambridge running June and November series and Pearson running May/June and November. Some subjects are tiered, so the entry decision made in Year 10 sets a grade ceiling before any revision begins. Syllabus codes differ by board even where the subject name does not.
programmes.countryNote: The gap at IGCSE is practice volume. A school will work through perhaps two or three past papers per subject in class across Year 11, which is nowhere near enough to build pace. A student aiming at the top grades on this coast should expect to sit eight to twelve full papers per subject independently, marked against the official mark scheme rather than self-assessed.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria marked out of eight and reported on a 1-7 scale. There is no external paper until the optional eAssessment, so progress is read entirely from criterion descriptors and teacher judgement rather than from exam marks.
programmes.countryNote: MYP parents on this coast are often the last to know there is a problem, because a 5 against criteria reads like a comfortable grade. The useful question to ask the school is which criteria the 5 is built from: a student strong on criterion A knowledge and weak on criterion C communicating is heading for difficulty in Diploma paper answers, and the single reported number hides it.

programmes.name: IB Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, transdisciplinary and unexamined. The useful measures at this stage are reading fluency, number-fact recall and written stamina, all of which can be tested quickly and improved with short, frequent practice rather than long sessions.
programmes.countryNote: The gap that matters in primary on this coast is written stamina. Children who can discuss an idea fluently but cannot sustain a paragraph arrive in Year 7 behind, and the deficit compounds through MYP into Diploma essay subjects. Twenty minutes of timed writing twice a week closes it faster than any amount of additional content.

ras-al-khaimah/al-marjan-island.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones where the independent-study gap is widest: heavy-content sciences, the two Diploma maths routes, and the essay subjects where structure rather than knowledge decides the band.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Energetics, equilibria and organic mechanisms carry the marks and reward repeated practice rather than rereading. Higher Level students most often lose marks in multi-step calculations where rounding propagates, and in mechanism questions where curly arrows are drawn approximately.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: The highest content volume of any science and the subject where revision method matters most. Extended-response questions want a named mechanism and precise terminology; students who revise by reading score consistently below those who answer past questions and compare against the mark scheme.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Circuits and electromagnetism stall IGCSE students; fields, thermodynamics and the quantum topic stall Higher Level ones. The uncertainty and data-analysis strand is rarely taught explicitly, is worth real marks, and is quick to repair once a student has seen how it is credited.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency. Marks disappear in the unstructured later questions where the topic is recognised but no method is prompted, and in the exploration where the mathematics is correct but the personal engagement and reflection criteria are thin.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics, modelling and calculator-led problem solving. Hypothesis testing, chi-squared and regression are the topics students most often meet properly for the first time in a mock. A surprising share of lost marks are calculator operation errors rather than mathematical ones.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE)
subjects.description: The Core and Extended decision caps the available grade, so it matters more than any single topic. Extended candidates drop marks in algebraic fractions, graph transformations and the long multi-mark problems where no structure is given.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Three internal assessment commentaries and diagram accuracy decide most grades. Evaluation written without reference to the diagram just drawn stops earning marks at the top band, and Higher Level quantitative questions reward legible working more than speed.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is unseen analysis under time pressure and rewards a repeatable structure. The Individual Oral needs a global issue narrow enough to argue in ten minutes. Students here usually have ideas and lack paragraph architecture, which is the faster thing to fix.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Command terms do most of the work. Answering 'evaluate' as though it were 'outline' loses the top band without writing anything incorrect. The Higher Level research project needs a real organisation and a question narrow enough to answer with available data.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Trace tables and pseudocode discipline account for a large share of IGCSE marks. The Higher Level internal assessment needs a genuine client and a bounded problem, and students who start coding before scoping lose criterion marks that are difficult to recover later.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Mandatory in UAE private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum. Progress comes from short, frequent practice aligned to the school's own prescribed scheme, since the Ministry's content requirements may not be substituted with alternative material.

ras-al-khaimah/al-marjan-island.regionsIntro: Students taught across this part of the emirate come from the island itself and from the coastal and city districts either side of the causeway. The notes record what changes for each: school feed, journey length and how the week is shaped.

regions.name: Al Marjan Island
regions.note: Four reclaimed fronds of apartment towers, hotel residences and villa plots. One causeway serves the whole island, so a delay there moves the start of an afternoon session for every family on it at once.

regions.name: Al Hamra Village
regions.note: The nearest mainland community and the location of the RAK Academy campuses. Most island families feed into these schools, which makes a shared syllabus and a shared internal deadline calendar common across island households.

regions.name: Mina Al Arab and Hayat Island
regions.note: Lagoon-side villas and newer apartments just south. Families here sit in the same school catchment as the island and face the same small Higher Level sets at Diploma level.

regions.name: Al Jazirah Al Hamra
regions.note: South towards Umm Al Quwain, with the heritage village and newer residential plots. A proportion of families here commute to Dubai schools, which changes the whole shape of the week.

regions.name: Al Nakheel
regions.note: The city's commercial centre and the base for most Indian-curriculum schools and tuition centres. Families crossing the causeway to reach it are making a round trip of close to an hour outside peak.

regions.name: Khuzam
regions.note: Inland residential district with a RAK Academy campus, mixing villas and apartment blocks. A common school destination for both island and city families.

regions.name: Al Dhait North and South

regions.note: Fishing and residential communities north of the city. Journeys to the southern coastal schools are long enough that boarding the school bus before seven is normal.

schoolClusters.note: The IB side of the emirate. The RAK Academy campuses run the continuum from primary through to the Diploma, and island families overwhelmingly feed into them. Higher Level sets are small, which concentrates the independent-study burden.

modes.description: One or two fixed sessions a week spent on the work the class has already covered, not ahead of it. The session is driven by the student's attempted problems and marked homework, which turns the taught content into something retrievable under exam conditions.

modes.description: A structured run of full past papers sat to time across a term, each marked against the official mark scheme and reviewed in the following session. This is the single most reliable way to close a mock-to-final gap, and almost no school has room to do it at volume.

modes.description: Scheduled support across the months an internal assessment or the Extended Essay runs. sections.heading: What a class of twenty covers, and what it leaves to the student
paragraphs: A scheme of work is written to deliver a syllabus in the available periods. It is not written to make every student in the room secure in every topic, because that is not achievable at a single pace. The result is a well-taught course with predictable residue: the topics that were covered in the week of a school trip, the ones taught just before a holiday, and the ones a particular student happened to be unwell for.

At IGCSE the residue is manageable if it is identified. Most of it shows up as specific topics rather than general weakness, and a diagnostic on past-paper questions will locate it in an hour. The error families make is treating a mock grade as a verdict on the subject rather than as a map of six or seven recoverable topics.

At Diploma level the residue is structural rather than topical. Internal assessment, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge are each the student's own project, and on a small campus the supervising teacher may be supervising six essays in six different fields. The student who waits to be told what to do next will be told late.

The table separates what schools reliably handle from what the student has to own. It is deliberately unflattering to nobody: the right-hand column is not a criticism of a school, it is the part of the course that was always designed to be independent work, and the part that tuition is genuinely useful for.

sections.heading: The independent study hours nobody puts on a timetable
paragraphs: Taught hours are published; independent hours are assumed. The IB's own guidance frames a Higher Level subject as 240 teaching hours across two years and a Standard Level subject as 150, and those figures describe contact time rather than the total work a grade requires. The difference is made up at home, and most students underestimate it by a factor of two.

A practical rule that holds across both programmes on this coast: for every taught hour in an exam subject, expect between forty and sixty minutes of independent work during normal term time, rising sharply in the eight weeks before a terminal series. For a Year 11 student with nine subjects that arithmetic is uncomfortable, which is precisely why it should be done in September rather than discovered in March.

The time goes missing in predictable ways. Homework set to be handed in gets done; revision with no deadline does not. Reading notes feels productive and produces little. An hour spent on a topic already secure is an hour not spent on the one that is not. And on this island specifically, families who drive to a tuition centre lose a further two to three hours a week to the causeway and the road into the city.
The table gives a workable weekly target by stage. The fourth column is the one worth discussing with your child, because every family recognises at least two of the leaks listed there.

sections.heading: The tier decision in Year 10 that sets the grade ceiling
paragraphs: Some Cambridge IGCSE subjects are tiered, and the entry a school makes decides the highest grade a student can be awarded before any revision happens. Mathematics 0580 is the clearest case: a Core entry caps the outcome, while an Extended entry opens the top grades and adds content and difficulty. Similar structures exist across several of the sciences and languages.

The decision is usually taken by the school on the basis of Year 10 performance, and it is often communicated to parents as an administrative note rather than as the strategic choice it is. Families on this coast frequently learn which tier their child is entered for only when the entry statement is issued, by which point moving between tiers means catching up on content that the Core set never saw.

The honest position is that neither tier is the right answer for every student. A Core entry achieved comfortably is a better outcome than an Extended entry that collapses, and for a child who needs five subjects at grade E or 3 for Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a secure Core pass may be exactly the correct plan. The mistake is making the decision by default.

Ask three questions before February of Year 10: which tier is my child currently entered for, what evidence is that based on, and what would need to change for the other tier to be viable. A tutor's job at that point is to tell you honestly whether the gap is closable in the time available, not to encourage the more expensive answer.

sections.heading: The internal assessment calendar most schools never hand out
paragraphs: Every Diploma student has two calendars. The first is the school's, with its internal deadlines for drafts and submissions. The second is the one that actually determines the grade: the sequence of decisions that have to be made months earlier for the deadline to be met with something good. Most schools publish the first and leave the second implicit.

The practical consequence on this coast is familiar. A student in DP1 is told the internal assessment is due in the autumn of DP2 and hears that as permission to think about it later. The topic is chosen in a hurry, the data collection is compressed, and the analysis is written in a fortnight. The work is submitted on time and scores in the middle bands because the design was rushed, not because the student is weak.

The Extended Essay follows the same pattern with a harder deadline. It is capped at 4,000 words, is supervised rather than taught, and requires a research question narrow enough to answer and broad enough to sustain an argument. Choosing that question is the single highest-leverage hour of the whole Diploma, and it is routinely done in twenty minutes.

The table below is the backwards version: each milestone paired with what must already exist by then. It is written for a May-session candidate, which is the session virtually every UAE school sits. No specific IB dates are published here, because the IB's own calendar should be confirmed with your school's Diploma coordinator rather than taken from a tutoring page.

sections.heading: Where the marks go between the mock and the real paper
paragraphs: A two-grade gap between a mock and a prediction is rarely a knowledge gap. Mocks are sat under lighter conditions, often on a shortened paper, sometimes with a teacher who has flagged the topics. The real paper removes all of that, and what it exposes is technique: pacing, command-term reading, working shown or not shown, and the discipline of attempting the last question at all.

Pacing is the biggest single loss. A student who spends eleven minutes on a four-mark opening question has already forfeited the marks at the end of the paper. The fix is mechanical and unglamorous: a mark-per-minute target written at the top of the page, and enough timed papers to make it automatic. It is also the reason a tutoring programme without timed papers tends to plateau.

Command terms account for the second tranche. 'State' wants a sentence, 'explain' wants a mechanism, 'evaluate' wants a judgement supported both ways. Students who answer every question at the same depth lose marks in both directions, writing too much on recall and too little on analysis. Mark schemes make this visible within one session, which is why they are read openly rather than kept on the tutor's side of the screen.

The table names each loss and what repairs it. The right-hand column matters because the repairs are not equally expensive: some take a fortnight, and one of them takes an exam season. Reading it in order also gives a sensible sequence, since pacing and command-term work pay back fastest and should be fixed before any attempt is made on the slower structural problems further down.

sections.heading: What closing the gap costs, in AED and in hours
paragraphs: No rate table has been published for Ras Al Khaimah. Every AED figure available in this market comes from a Dubai source, so the bands below are reported with the provider that publishes them and should be read as a ceiling rather than as a local quote. Families in this emirate commonly report paying at or below the Dubai mid-band for an equivalently qualified teacher.

Rate alone is the wrong basis for a decision. The useful question is cost per unit of the gap closed. A budget hour spent re-explaining content already understood is expensive; a specialist hour spent on marked timed papers and criterion feedback is not. That is also why the formats in the previous sections are priced differently in practice: a timed-paper programme needs marking time, and internal assessment coaching is spread thinly across months.

IB Gram does not publish a fixed hourly price on these pages, because the honest figure depends on the subject, the level and how many sessions a week a student needs. A consultation establishes the plan, a trial lesson tests the match, and the quote follows. Nothing on this page is an IB Gram price.

For budget context, KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not increase for the 2026-27 academic year under the emirate's second economic incentives package. Fee policy is set emirate by emirate, so check your own school's position with it and with the Department of Knowledge rather than assuming the Dubai announcement applies here.
